passages.text: A transdiagnostic approach to understanding neural responsivity to reward and its links to social motivation

Schizophrenia (SZ) and bipolar disorder (BD) are characterized by social impairments. Social impairment also occurs in the general community. Across clinical and nonclinical groups social impairment may be related to deficits in social approach and/or social avoidance motivation. However, the neural basis of social motivation deficits in SZ and BD is not well understood, nor is it known if they reflect features of the illness or are secondary to other factors such as social isolation. To fill these knowledge gaps, 31 individuals with SZ, 27 with BD, and 42 community comparisons (CCs) completed a team-based task during fMRI in which positive and negative feedback was provided by pictures of teammates or opponents. Importantly, the CC group was enriched for self-reported social isolation. fMRI analyses in five key regions of interest (ROIs; ventral striatum, orbital frontal cortex, insula, dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, amygdala), secondary whole-brain analyses, and associations between ROI activity and social approach/avoidance motivation were performed. Across groups, ventral striatum and amygdala showed greater activation to positive versus negative feedback. In SZ, ventral striatum activity to positive feedback was correlated with social approach motivation. In CCs, amygdala activity during negative feedback was correlated with social avoidance motivation. Whole-brain analyses revealed greater activation in BD compared to SZ and CCs in fronto-parietal regions when feedback was provided by an opponent. Findings support disturbed reward sensitivity as a core component of poor social approach motivation in SZ and offer avenues for future research into neural mechanisms underlying social impairment in BD and the general community.
Highlights
Social impairments occur in serious mental illness and the general community.
Deficits in social motivation may be contributing factors.
In schizophrenia, ventral striatum activity to reward was linked to social approach.
In isolated controls amygdala activity to punishment was linked to social avoidance.
Introduction

Social impairment is common among individuals with serious mental illnesses (SMI), including schizophrenia (SZ) and bipolar disorder (BD). For example, people with SZ tend to be socially isolated (e.g.,) with few social contacts and a lack of meaningful social relationships (i.e., close friends and family). Although people with BD are generally less socially impaired than those with SZ, BD is also associated with compromised social support and strained relationships. In BD, greater social impairment is associated with increased mood symptom severity, suicidality, and higher rates of relapse.

Social impairment is also prevalent in the general population. For example, social isolation is relatively common in nonclinical samples, where it is associated with poorer cognitive, mental, and physical health, including increased mortality. Social impairment in SMI and members of the general community may be driven by deficits in social motivation.

Social motivation is the drive to form and maintain social bonds, reflecting the direction, intensity, and persistence of socially-oriented behaviors. Social motivation can be divided into two major categories: social approach motivation and social avoidance motivation. Social approach motivation promotes engagement and attachment, reflecting an orientation toward socially rewarding or desired outcomes (e.g., companionship, acceptance, intimacy). In the brain, this system primarily involves the ventral striatum (VS) and orbital frontal cortex (OFC), regions implicated in reward processing. Dopaminergic and opioid signaling within this neural system are thought to underlie pleasurable, subjective feelings of social connectedness. This system is also rich in oxytocin receptors, promoting the salience of social cues. On the whole, the social approach motivation system promotes expectation of positive social outcomes and enhances approach-related attachment behaviors. Conversely, low social approach motivation is typically referred to as social anhedonia in the schizophrenia literature.

Social avoidance motivation, in contrast to social approach, is focused on moving away from socially punishing, undesirable, or threatening outcomes (e.g., rejection, betrayal, discord). In the brain, this system primarily involves the insula, dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC), and amygdala, regions implicated in threat detection, risk assessment, and conflict monitoring. Context-dependent modulation of dopaminergic and opioid signaling in these pathways is implicated in threat avoidance and pain regulation. Social approach and avoidance systems can be examined during functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) using paradigms designed to reveal the extent to which social stimuli are perceived as rewarding (e.g., the stimulus elicits approach behavior) versus threatening or aversive (e.g., the stimulus elicits avoidance behavior).

Studies of SMI samples consistently show altered responses to both positive and negative social feedback. For example, individuals with SZ tend to devalue socially rewarding stimuli (e.g., smiles) and demonstrate reduced responsivity to praise. Response to socially aversive stimuli, such as angry faces, is also altered in SZ. Although social reward processing has not been as extensively studied in BD, findings indicate enhanced reactivity to both rewarding and aversive social cues. Direct links to social motivation processes have not been examined in prior literature.

In particular, two previous sets of findings guided the current work. First, we previously found that a community sample of individuals who were socially isolated tended to be even more isolated, lonelier, and reported even greater levels of social anhedonia than individuals with SZ, thus demonstrating marked social impairment. The neural basis of social impairment in this population has not been previously studied. Further, we found that in a broad sample of psychosis spectrum disorders, lower activity in key social approach motivation brain regions, including VS, during a team-based social reward task was associated with increased self-reported social anhedonia. This association was not seen in unaffected siblings or non-psychiatric comparison participants. It is not clear whether associations between neural activity within the social motivation system and self-report trait measures of social anhedonia and social avoidance motivation are specific to psychosis spectrum disorders or might extend to other conditions with known social impairments, such as BD. It is also not known whether these associations between neural activity and social factors exist in community samples that are recruited specifically to be enriched for social isolation.

Thus, the aims of the current study were twofold. For one, we wanted to investigate the neural basis of social motivation across clinical and nonclinical groups with observable social deficits; namely, individuals with SZ, individuals with BD, and socially isolated members of the general community (CCs). Second, we wanted to test for associations between social motivation-related neural activity and self-report measures of social motivation in those three samples. Overall, this approach allowed us to determine whether social isolation is related to neural markers of altered social approach and/or social avoidance motivation across clinical and nonclinical groups and whether they reflect features of the illness or are secondary to social isolation.

To achieve these aims we utilized a team-based task during fMRI that provides both positive and negative social feedback from individuals designated as "teammates" or "opponents". The task was designed to index neural activity reflective of how rewarding or aversive participants found the positive and negative feedback provided by the other players, depending on team status (i.e., whether they were teammates or opponents). The team aspect of the task was thus intended to approximate in-group/out-group dynamics, with the possible generation of social affiliation toward fellow in-group members (teammates) and bias or animosity against out-group members (opponents). We compared fMRI activity in individuals with SZ, individuals with BD, and CCs in key regions of the social approach and social avoidance networks (i.e., VS, OFC, amygdala, dACC, insula). We hypothesized that, 1) the SZ group would show intermediate responsivity within social-approach motivation neural circuitry in response to rewarding social feedback, between CC (lowest responsivity) and BD (highest responsivity) groups; and 2) the SZ and BD groups would show elevated responsivity within the social-avoidance motivation neural circuitry in response to aversive social feedback compared to the CC group. Further, based on our previous findings, we hypothesized that, 3) neural activation of social-approach motivation circuitry during rewarding social feedback would be associated with self-reported social approach motivation in all three groups; and 4) neural activation of social-avoidance motivation circuitry during aversive social feedback would be associated with self-reported social avoidance motivation in all three groups.
Methods
Participants

This study was part of a larger project designed to understand whether social motivation deficits in two clinical populations, SZ and BD, are attributable to the disorders themselves or a personal history of social isolation. In this paper we present data from the fMRI portion of the project that included 31 individuals with SZ, 30 individuals with BD, and 43 community comparisons (CCs). Importantly, the community sample was enriched for self-reported social isolation (see below for recruitment details). Overall, four individuals were excluded due to missing data (3 BD: technical issues during two scans resulted in data being corrupted/not recorded properly; one participant did not complete the scan due to anxiety. 1 CC: participant did not complete the scan due to anxiety), leaving a final sample of 31 SZ, 27 BD, and 42 CC. The two clinical samples were recruited from outpatient clinics at the Veterans Affairs Greater Los Angeles Healthcare System (GLA) and the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), as well as outpatient board and care facilities in the Greater Los Angeles area. The Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-5 (SCID-5) was administered to establish/confirm diagnoses. Medical records were also used to corroborate diagnoses when needed. All SZ and BD participants were clinically stable, with no hospitalizations within the prior three months and no changes in psychiatric medication type/dosage within four weeks. Both clinical samples were receiving psychiatric medications as prescribed by their providers at the time of assessment.

Advertisements posted online were used to recruit a community sample with elevated social isolation. The ads asked: "Do you have few friends, little contact with family members, and typically do activities alone?" We also ran online ads for control participants that were similar to those used in our previous studies and did not mention social isolation or connection. The community sample, as a whole, was thus enriched for social isolation, with 63 % of the participants in this group responding to the first ad and reporting having little social contact with friends and family.

All participants in the community sample were administered the SCID-5 as well as portions of the SCID for Personality Disorders (SCID-PD) to assess for avoidant, paranoid, schizoid, schizotypal, and borderline characteristics. Participants in this group were excluded if they met the criteria for a lifetime history of a psychotic disorder or bipolar disorder, but personality disorder diagnoses were not exclusionary. All study procedures were approved by the Institutional Review Boards of GLA and UCLA, and all participants provided written informed consent.

Inclusion criteria for all participants were: (a) age 20-60, (b) understanding of English to a sufficient level to comprehend procedures, (c) no clinically significant neurological disease (e.g. epilepsy), (d) no history of a serious head injury (loss of consciousness >1 h), (e) no sedatives or benzodiazepines within 12 h of testing, (f) no evidence of IQ < 70 or developmental disability based on the Wide-Range Achievement Test 3rd ed. reading subtest, (g) no substance use disorder at moderate level or greater in the past three months, and (h) no current mood episode meeting clinical criteria for depression, hypomania, or mania, (i) expressed willingness to participate in neuroimaging and no contraindications for an MRI scan.
Assessment of social isolation

To examine the level of social isolation among the samples, we used a standardized composite of three complementary scales: (1) Lubben Social Network Scale (12 item version), (2) Social Disconnectedness Scale (last 4 items), and (3) the Role Functioning Scale (social and family scores). Scores were converted as needed so that larger values on this composite variable indicated greater social isolation. For further information on the calculation of the composite, including its reliability, see.
Assessment of clinical symptoms

In addition to diagnostic interviews, clinical symptoms were rated for the psychiatric samples using the Expanded Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale (BPRS), the Clinical Assessment Interview for Negative Symptoms (CAINS), the Hamilton Depression Scale, and the Young Mania Rating Scale. Training and quality assurance on all interviews were conducted through established procedures by the Treatment Unit of the Department of Veterans Affairs VISN 22 Mental Illness Research Education and Clinical Center (MIRECC).
Assessment of social motivation

Social approach motivation was measured using a version of the Social Anhedonia Scale (SAS), a well-validated scale that is widely used in SZ research. This version of the SAS contains 24-item true-false self-report items which assess different components of social anhedonia that reflect both anticipation and consummatory experience (i.e., wanting and liking), including social pleasure (e.g., "Just being with friends can make me feel really good" - reverse scored); interest in social connections ("Having close friends is not as important as many people say"), aloofness ("People often expect me to spend more time talking with them than I would like"); and preference for solitude and solo activities ("I prefer hobbies and leisure activities that do not involve other people"). Responses were scored dichotomously on a scale from 0 to 24, with higher scores reflecting greater social anhedonia or lower social approach motivation.

Social avoidance motivation was measured using the Sensitivity to Rejection Scale (SRS). This scale includes 24 items that assess distinct factors: the avoidance of situations or actions that could lead to contentious or critical exchanges (e.g., "I criticize people openly and expect them to do the same"); apprehension about sharing personal views for fear of rejection (e.g., "When a group is discussing an important matter, I like my feelings to be known"); hesitance to make requests or impose on others (e.g., "I often visit people without being invited"); susceptibility to being hurt by negative criticism and avoidance of such situations (e.g., "I would be very hurt if a close friend should contradict me in public"); and the preference for the company of familiar individuals to prevent rejection (e.g., "I sometimes prefer being with strangers than with familiar people"). Responses were recorded using a 9-point scale ranging from -4 (very strong disagreement) to +4 (very strong agreement). For this study, we used a total score ranging from -96 to +96, with higher scores indicating greater social avoidance.
fMRI task

Participants completed a team-based dot counting task during fMRI. Briefly, the participant's goal in the task was to win as many trials as possible for their team by correctly selecting which side of the computer screen displayed more dots. Responses (left/right) were recorded using a button box. After each trial, participants received written feedback on the outcome of their task performance that was either positive (WON!) or negative (LOST!) paired with the expressive face of a teammate or opponent. The face stimuli for teammates and opponents were drawn from a standardized emotional stimulus set (Karolinska Directed Emotional Faces set; KDEF). The teammates' faces were happy for wins and angry for losses (i.e., congruent with trial outcome), whereas opponents' faces were angry for wins and happy for losses (i.e., incongruent with trial outcome). Prior to the MRI scan, each participant was informed of the team-based aspects of the game and introduced to the faces of their teammates and opponents. Time was taken to ensure they thoroughly understood the game and were familiar with the other players.

In addition to the primary win/loss test trials, the task also included a neutral control condition in which the feedback was replaced by a scrambled image paired with the word "REDO." For control trials, neither team won or lost a point. In total, the task consisted of 100 test trials (50 trials with feedback from a teammate and 50 trials with feedback from an opponent) and 25 control trials across five runs. Each trial sequence included a central fixation cross (jittered duration: range: 3000 ms to 7000 ms), dot array presentation (500 ms), response period (up to up to 4000 ms), and feedback (1500 ms). Total scan time, including four built-in rest periods, was approximately 25 min.
MRI acquisition and preprocessing

Scanning was performed on a 3-Tesla Siemens MAGNETOM Prisma-FIT scanner at the UCLA Staglin Center for Cognitive Neuroscience. A high-resolution T1-weighted magnetization prepared rapid-acquisition gradient echo image (MPRAGE) was acquired from each subject for anatomical localization and registration of functional data [TR = 2000 ms; TE = 2.52 ms; flip angle = 12 ; 192 sagittal slices; slice thickness = 1.0 mm; matrix = 256 x 256; FOV = 256 mm; voxel size = 1.0 x 1.0 x 1.0 mm]. Five fMRI runs were acquired with T2*-weighted blood oxygen level-dependent (BOLD) gradient echo planar imaging (EPI) sequences during the task (TR = 700 ms, TE = 33 ms, flip angle = 50 , 54 interleaved slices, slice thickness = 2.5 mm; matrix = 76.8 x 76.8; FOV = 192 mm; voxel size = 2.5 x 2.5 x 2.5 mm).

Raw MRI DICOM file images were converted to NIFTI format and organized into the Brain Imaging Data Structure using HeuDiConv (https://github.com/nipy/heudiconv). Data preprocessing was then performed using fMRIPrep v.22.0.2. The full description of this preprocessing (comprising the boilerplate text automatically generated by the fMRIprep software) is provided in Supplementary Materials. Additional details on fMRIPrep preprocessing pipelines are available in online documentation (https://fmriprep.org).

Briefly, individual T1-weighted structural images were intensity corrected, skull stripped, and normalized to MNI ICBM 152 non-linear asymmetrical template (MNI152NLin6Asym) using ANTs 2.3.3. Brain tissue segmentation was performed using fast (FSL 6.0.5) and brain surface reconstruction used FreeSurfer 7.2.0. For functional BOLD data, head-motion parameters were estimated using mcflirt (FSL 6.0.5). Functional images were slice-time corrected using 3dTshif (AFNI), and co-registered to the T1-weighted reference using bbregister (Freesurfer) then resampled into standard space. A high-pass temporal filter (128 s cut-off) and a spatial smooth (6 mm FWHM) were then applied to data from each run. Finally, automatic removal of motion artifacts was performed using independent component analysis (ICA-AROMA) on preprocessed BOLD data. Confound timeseries (derived from head motion estimates) and additional nuisance timeseries were included later in first-level modeling to further clean the functional data.
Brain parcellation and ROI definition

Location of regions-of-interest (ROI). Bilateral cortical (orbital frontal cortex, OFC; dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, dACC; insula, INS) and subcortical (ventral striatum, VS; amygdala, AMYG) ROI were defined for each participant based on individual parcellation maps normalized to standard space. Locations from a sample participant are shown. Slice location provided in Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) coordinates.
Fig. 1

Statistical tests of the primary study hypotheses relied on data from specific cortical (OFC, dACC, insula) and subcortical (amygdala, VS) ROIs. All ROIs were defined bilaterally. To define the ROIs, we used the automated anatomical segmentation of these regions on each participant's high-resolution scans from the FreeSurfer preprocessing performed by fMRIprep (see Supplementary Materials for details). Note that for OFC, the ROI we used included both lateral and medial aspects. ROIs were visually inspected to ensure accuracy. Relevant cortical and subcortical anatomical region labels were then projected into each subject's functional (EPI) space to create volumetric ROIs from which mean beta values were extracted. See Fig. 1 for example ROI locations from an individual participant.
fMRI data analysis

Analysis of fMRI data was performed with FSL-FEAT (FMRI Expert Analysis Tool v6.0), part of the FMRIB Software Library (FSL v6.0.4; Analysis Group, Oxford, UK), using a general linear model (GLM) approach and a timing model based on a double-gamma hemodynamic response function. In the first-level analysis, linear contrasts of trials by condition were created for each subject (see Supplementary Table S1 for a complete list of contrasts included in the GLM). We conducted a 2 x 2 analysis by group: trial outcome (WON versus LOST) x team (TEAMMATE versus OPPONENT), with each experimental condition contrasted against the neutral trials as a baseline control condition. Mean beta values from the five key ROIs during feedback on test versus neutral control trials were analyzed using repeated measures ANOVAs to compare within- and between-group activation across the task conditions. A two-tailed Bonferroni-adjusted significance threshold for each test was applied, corresponding to p < .01 for each of the five ROIs.

In addition to the primary ROI analyses, we also conducted a secondary voxel-wise whole-brain analysis with FSL. The contrasts of WON trials > LOST trials and the reverse (LOST > WON) were used to examine the main effects of trial outcome. The contrasts of TEAMMATE > OPPONENT and the reverse (OPPONENT > TEAMMATE) were used to examine the main effects of team status. The five runs per task for each participant were averaged together in a fixed effects model. These averages were then entered into a random-effects model for analysis by diagnostic group, using FLAME (FMRIB's Local Analysis of Mixed Effects) stage 1 module. Variance estimates were calculated for each group separately. We report clusters exceeding a Z of 2.3 and a cluster probability of p < .05, corrected for whole-brain multiple comparisons.

Associations with measures of social motivation were analyzed in R (Version 4.2.0) and figures were generated using the ggplot2 package (Version 3.3.5). We examined associations within each diagnostic group between 1) ROI activity during positive/reward feedback (i.e., wins) and self-reported social anhedonia (i.e., SAS total scores) and 2) ROI activity during negative/aversive feedback (i.e., losses) and self-reported social avoidance motivation (i.e., SRS total scores) in ROIs that showed significant effects of the task manipulations. Correction for multiple comparisons was conducted within each sample separately using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate procedure. If any correlations were statistically significant after correction, we used Fischer's r-to-z transformation to examine differences in coefficient magnitude between groups.

BPRS = Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale; CAINS = Clinical Assessment Interview for Negative Symptoms; MAP = Motivation and Pleasure; HAM-D = Hamilton Depression Scale; YMRS = Young Mania Rating Scale; SAS = Social Anhedonia Scale; SRS = Sensitivity to Rejection Scale.

Demographic and clinical data are listed in Table 1. There was a significant difference among the three groups in years of personal education and parental education. The SZ group had fewer years of personal education than either the BD or CC groups (p = .01 and p < .001, respectively). The BD group had greater years of parental education than the CC group (p = .04). There were no significant differences between groups in terms of age, sex, race, or ethnicity. The SZ group had mild to moderate symptoms. The BD group were all in a euthymic state with minimal mood symptoms.
Social isolation, loneliness, and social motivation data

Social isolation, loneliness, and social motivation self-report data are listed in Table 1. There were no significant differences among the three groups on the social isolation composite variable [F (2, 96) = 2.48, p = .09], suggesting that the community sample was indeed enriched for social isolation and on par with the clinical samples. There were no significant differences among the groups in terms of self-reported loneliness [F (2, 96) = 1.46, p = .24]. There were no significant differences among the groups on self-reported social anhedonia (SAS total scores) [F (2, 96) = 0.91, p = .41] or social avoidance motivation (SRS total scores) [F (2, 96) = 2.80, p = .07]. Intercorrelations between the clinical and social measures are provided in Supplementary Table S2.
ROI analyses

Ventral striatum activity and associations with social anhedonia. A.) Boxplots of bilateral ventral striatum (VS) activity (dots denote each participant's mean beta values) for WON and LOST trials by group. Within each box, horizontal lines denote the group median; boxes extend from the 25th to the 75th percentile of each group's distribution of values. There was significantly greater activation to WON feedback [whether paired with a teammate (smiling face) or opponent (angry face)] compared to LOST feedback [whether paired with a teammate (angry face) or opponent (smiling face)]. B.) Associations by group between Social Anhedonia Scale (SAS) scores and activity in VS for WON feedback. Among the SZ group only, lower VS activity was associated with higher SAS scores (i.e., less social approach motivation).
Fig. 2

Amygdala activity and associations with social avoidance motivation. A.) Boxplots of bilateral amygdala activity (dots denote each participant's mean beta values) for WON and LOST trials by group. Within each box, horizontal lines denote the group median; boxes extend from the 25th to the 75th percentile of each group's distribution of values. There was significantly greater activation to WON feedback [whether paired with a teammate (smiling face) or opponent (angry face)] compared to LOST feedback [whether paired with a teammate (angry face) or opponent (smiling face)]. B.) Associations by group between Sensitivity to Rejection Scale (SRS) scores and activity in amygdala for LOST feedback. Among the community group only, higher amygdala activity was associated with higher SRS scores (i.e., greater social avoidance motivation).
Fig. 3

For VS and amygdala there was a significant main effect of trial outcome, with greater activation for WON trials versus LOST trials [VS: F (1, 97) = 43.21, p < .001, etap2 = 0.31, Fig. 2A; amygdala: F (1, 97) = 6.71, p = .01, etap2 = 0.07, Fig. 3A] regardless of whether the feedback was provided by a teammate or an opponent (i.e., no effect of team status). There were no significant main effects or interactions involving diagnostic group (SZ, BD, CC) or team status for VS or amygdala. There were no significant effects in OFC, dACC, or insula for trial outcome, team status, or diagnostic group that survived correction for multiple comparisons.
Whole-brain analyses

Detailed results of the exploratory whole-brain analyses are in Supplemental Materials (Supplementary Table S3). Briefly, in terms of the main effects of trial outcome, all groups showed extensive BOLD activity in response to WON > LOST feedback in regions associated with social and reward processing, including VS, amygdala, medial prefrontal cortex, and posterior cingulate cortex. In response to LOST > WON feedback, all groups showed significant BOLD activity in several frontal regions as well as anterior insula. There were no significant pair-wise between-group differences for either WON vs LOST contrasts.

For the main effects of team status, all groups showed significant BOLD activity in response to OPPONENT > TEAMMATE (i.e., feedback provided by an opponent versus a teammate) in several fronto-parietal regions. See Supplementary Table S3 for details. Pair-wise group comparisons of the OPPONENT > TEAMMATE contrast revealed that BD showed significantly greater activation compared to SZ in bilateral precuneus and greater activation compared to CCs in dACC, right supramarginal gyrus, angular gyrus, and frontal pole (see also Supplementary Fig. S1). In response to TEAMMATE > OPPONENT (i.e., feedback provided by a teammate versus an opponent) only CCs showed significant BOLD activity, in bilateral central opercular cortex and Heschl's gyrus. No pair-wise between-group differences reached the significance threshold for the TEAMMATE > OPPONENT contrast.

We examined Pearson correlations between self-reported social anhedonia and social avoidance motivation and fMRI activity corresponding to significant effects of the primary experimental conditions of the task. Specifically, we examined the following 12 correlations (4 in each sample): 1) VS activity during WON trials and SAS scores; 2) VS activity during LOST trials and SRS scores; 3) amygdala activity during WON trials and SAS scores; and 4) amygdala activity during LOST trials and SRS scores (see Table 2 and Supplementary Table S4). After correcting for multiple comparisons, there was a significant correlation within the SZ group between VS activity during WON trials and SAS scores, such that higher VS activity was associated with lower SAS scores (r = -0.46, pcorrected = 0.034; Fig. 2, panel B). This correlation was significantly larger in the SZ sample compared to CCs (r = 0.08; z = -2.34, p = .02); but not compared to the BP sample (r = -0.05; z = -1.66, p = .10). No other correlations were significant within the SZ sample. Within CCs, there was a significant correlation between amygdala activity during loss trials and social avoidance motivation, such that higher SRS scores were associated with greater amygdala activity (r = 0.38, pcorrected = 0.050; Fig. 3, panel B). This correlation in CCs was not significantly different from the correlation in the SZ sample (r = -0.02; z = 1.7, p = .09) or the BD sample (r = 0.25; z = 0.58, p = .56). No other correlations were significant within the community sample. No correlations were significant within the BD sample.
Discussion

In this study we examined neural activity within the social approach and avoidance motivation systems associated with a team-based reward task in individuals with SZ, those with BD, and a CC sample enriched for social isolation. Consistent with our previous findings we found significant effects related to trial outcome in VS and amygdala across groups, with greater activation during positive feedback (win trials) compared to negative feedback (loss trials). There were no significant task effects related to team status (i.e., in-group/out-group classification) in VS or amygdala, and no interactions by diagnostic group for either trial outcome or team status. We did not find any task-related effects or group interactions that survived correction for multiple comparisons in OFC, dACC, or insula.

Although there were no group differences in mean ROI activation levels, VS activity during positive feedback was significantly negatively associated with individual differences in social anhedonia among those with SZ. This finding mirrors and extend results of our previous work in which lower VS activity during positive feedback was associated with higher self-reported social anhedonia among individuals with psychosis spectrum disorders. That is, the extent to which VS responsivity to reward (a neural indicator of consummatory pleasure or in the moment "liking" of positive feedback) is blunted in individuals with SZ, the greater their social anhedonia, a measure of low social approach motivation. Of note, this finding was only observed in the group of patients with psychosis across both this and our prior study, indicating that reward sensitivity is more directly linked to social approach motivation in these individuals compared to other patient groups (e.g., the BD group) and other non-psychiatric groups that are socially isolated (e.g., the CC group). Taken together, this consistent finding across two separate samples highlights social reward processing in VS as a core component of social anhedonia in psychotic illness.

Further, in the current study we found that among the CC group, amygdala activity during loss feedback was significantly positively associated with self-reported social avoidance motivation. That is, among socially isolated community members, the more responsive amygdala activity was to loss (i.e., negative feedback), the higher their sensitivity to rejection, a measure of social avoidance motivation. These findings are not unexpected given the putative role of amygdala in emotional valence processing, threat detection, and monitoring. However, this correlation was only found in the community sample which was enriched for social isolation, and was not found in the healthy controls in the previous study. This finding raises the possibility that social isolation in this group may be partly due to discomfort in being around others (i.e., driven by social avoidance) as opposed to a reduced drive to approach others (i.e., driven by social anhedonia).

Although we did not find significant task or group-related effects in the BD group in the ROIs, whole-brain analyses revealed significantly greater activation compared to both SZ and CC groups in several regions related to team status. In particular, when feedback was provided by an opponent compared to a teammate, individuals with BD showed significantly greater activation compared to those with SZ in bilateral precuneus and greater activation compared to the CC sample in several fronto-parietal regions. The current findings of hyperactivity during incongruent, potentially aversive social feedback is consistent with prior neuroimaging studies in BD that have similarly demonstrated hyperactivity in ventral prefrontal cortex and dorsal anterior cingulate cortex in the context of social and emotion processing tasks. Whether heightened neural processing of other-oriented social information is directly tied to increased social avoidance motivation and sensitivity to social rejection in BD (e.g., requires further study. Due to the exploratory nature of these whole-brain analyses, we did not analyze correlations between activity in these additional regions and the self-report social motivation scales.

The current study is one of only a few attempts to experimentally manipulate in-group/out-group social dynamics in SZ and BD. Unfortunately, we did not find significant effects of team status (i.e., neural activity in response to trial outcome feedback did not vary depending on whether it was provided by a teammate or an opponent) in any of the ROIs. It may be that the relative strength of the win/loss trial outcome signal obscured signal related to team status because team status was nested within the win/loss outcome feedback. Alternatively, some participants may not have fully recalled the faces of their teammates versus those of their opponents, despite allocating sufficient time in the pre-task practice to ensure that participants understood the team-based aspect of the task. Future studies utilizing this type of task could include a manipulation check to ensure that participants remember the team status of the other players. In addition, the paired performance feedback (win/loss outcome presented along with happy/angry faces) did not allow us to fully tease apart social from non-social motivation processes. Future iterations of the task could provide social and non-social performance feedback separately rather than pairing them.

The study has some additional limitations. Our SZ patient sample was comprised of chronic outpatients and our BP patient sample was comprised of a mix of outpatients with BP I and BP II diagnoses. All patients were stable and on psychiatric medication as prescribed by their providers. It is thus not known whether similar patterns of findings would be observed in recent-onset or unmedicated samples, or in samples with higher levels of symptoms (e.g., in-episode BP patients). In addition, we do not know the precise nature or full extent of the social isolation among the CC group, beyond what may be indicated by their scores on our selection of measures (e.g., self-reported loneliness, measures of social approach and avoidance motivation). We intentionally did not recruit the community sample according to the reasons for the isolation (e.g., if they chose to isolate or not) nor did we make any assumptions about the nature of the isolation. Hence, these factors are not something that we can determine.

Finally, while the findings related to associations between ROI activity and social approach and avoidance measures are compelling, we note that those measures are self-report assessment tools and may involve response or memory bias. However, recent studies have assessed similar brain-behavior relationships with more real-world measures of social motivation such as ecological momentary assessment (EMA), and findings are consistent with ours. For example, found that reduced anticipatory motivation as assessed with EMA was associated with poorer reward-based learning and blunted anterior cingulate, insula, and striatal activation while anticipating reward. This EMA-based research that similarly links brain-behavior relationships in reward processing to real-world social functioning strengthens confidence in the current findings.

Despite the limitations, it is worth noting that an important strength of the current study is the unique feature of the CC sample. This community sample consisted of those who self-identified as socially isolated (roughly 2/3) and those who did not (roughly 1/3). Importantly, the CC sample was as socially isolated as the SZ and the BD samples. Hence, the current findings for neural activity and their correlations are not easily attributed to group differences in living with social isolation. Overall, the current findings suggest that a fundamental problem in social reward reflected by activation in the VS has motivational consequences reflected by self-report of social anhedonia in schizophrenia.

passages.text: Structural determinants of protease-activated receptor 1 cleavage by activated protein C
Background:

Activated protein C (APC) performs cytoprotective functions mediated by cleavage of the protease-activated receptor 1 (PAR1) in the presence of the endothelial protein C receptor and signaling through beta-arrestin-2. APC cleaves PAR1 at R41 and R46, but the specificity of the reaction is low. In contrast, thrombin cleaves PAR1 at R41 only in a reaction that is independent of endothelial protein C receptor, producing a proinflammatory response mediated by signaling through G-protein intermediates and features high specificity. The molecular basis of this difference between APC and thrombin remains unknown.
Objectives:
To identify the structural determinants of APC that influence PAR1 specificity.
Methods:

Using available structural information, we engineered thrombin determinants of PAR1 recognition into APC. Specifically, we replaced T99 with Leu and swapped the entire 37- and 60-loops of APC with those of thrombin (eg, APC60/T99L and APC37/60/T99L).
Results:

The engineered APC variants featured up to 80-fold enhanced specificity toward PAR1 mediated by increased cleavage at R41 and decreased cleavage at R46. Notably, the variants APC60/T99L and APC37/60/T99L also showed significantly reduced activity toward factor Va.
Conclusion:
The 37, 60, and 99 segments of APC determine the cytoprotective and anticoagulant properties of the enzyme.
INTRODUCTION

In addition to its procoagulant and prothrombotic roles mediated by cleavage of fibrinogen and the protease-activated receptor 1 (PAR1), thrombin functions as a potent inhibitor of coagulation by activating the zymogen protein C (PC) into the enzyme activated PC (APC), which itself is endowed with diverse physiological roles. As a natural anticoagulant, APC inactivates factor (F)Va and FVIIIa. As an anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective agent, APC signals through PAR1 to reduce cellular damage following sepsis and ischemia/reperfusion. The cytoprotective functions of APC depend on cleavage of PAR1 in the presence of the endothelial PC receptor (EPCR) and signaling through beta-arrestin-2. PAR1 is also activated by thrombin independently of EPCR and triggers a signaling pathway mediated by G-protein intermediates, resulting in a proinflammatory response and disruption of the endothelial barrier integrity. How cleavage of the same receptor, PAR1, leads to distinct signaling pathways remains unresolved at the molecular level. It has been proposed that PAR1 is cleaved at different sites by thrombin and APC, with the former cleaving exclusively at R41 and the latter cleaving at both R41 and R46. Cleavage at R46 is responsible for the beneficial cytoprotective function of APC.

Thrombin cleaves PAR1 with values of kcat/KM orders of magnitude faster than APC, and the difference likely depends on the determinants of PAR1 recognition in the 2 enzymes. The structure of thrombin bound to the extracellular fragment of PAR1 reveals that R41 is positioned within the active site. However, rather than binding to the active site, PAR1-R46 interacts with Q38 of thrombin, located in the 37-loop, which explains lack of cleavage at this site (Figure 1A). On the other hand, PAR1 cannot engage the 37-loop of APC in the same orientation as in thrombin due to steric clash between PAR1-R46 and K39 of APC (Figure 1A), which likely forces PAR1-R46 into the primary specificity pocket of APC for cleavage. Additional differences between the 2 enzymes involve the nature of the residue preceding the site of cleavage in PAR1, defined as the P2 residue, which is Pro (P40) for PAR1-R41 and Leu (L45) for PAR1-R46 (Figure 1D). Thrombin has a strong preference for Pro at P2 because of the hydrophobic nature of the recognition site of this residue, referred to as the S2 site, which is defined by the side chain of L99 and a long insertion in the 60-loop containing Y60a and W60d (Figure 1B). These 2 residues are part of the 60-loop of thrombin, which contains a 12-residue insertion that constrains the size of substrate that can be accommodated in the S2 site. In contrast, the 60-loop of APC is by 8 residues shorter than in thrombin and poses no hindrance to the S2 subsite. Consequently, the analogous S2 site of APC is hydrophilic and solvent accessible because of the shorter 60-loop and the presence of T99 that discriminates poorly between different residues at P2 and would show low affinity for P40 in the R41 site of PAR1 (Figure 1B). The foregoing differences between thrombin and APC suggest a simple strategy to engineer PAR1 specificity in APC to be more like thrombin.
METHODS

Expression and purification of PC were as described. PC variants (8 muM) were converted into APC upon incubation with 0.3 muM thrombin for 90 to 120 minutes at 37  C in 5 mM EDTA, 145 mM NaCl, 20 mM Tris, pH 7.5. After diluting NaCl < 50 mM, APC was loaded onto a Q-Sepharose (Cytiva) column equilibrated with 40 mM NaCl and 20 mM Tris, pH 7.5, and eluted using a 0 to 1 M NaCl gradient.

The active site concentration was quantified by monitoring the acyl-enzyme complex formation produced by reacting APC (100 nM) with the spectrofluorometric titrant 4-methylumbelliferyl 4-guanidinobenzoate (30 muM; Sigma-Aldrich). The release of 4-methylumbelliferone was continuously monitored (lambdaexcitation = 375 nm and lambdaemission = 445 nm) under experimental conditions of 200 nM hirudin, 110 mM NaCl, 20 mM HEPES, pH 7.5, at 7  C. The active site concentration was determined from the pre-steady-state burst formation of acyl-enzyme complex by referencing the change in fluorescence to a standard curve prepared with 4-methylumbelliferone (Sigma-Aldrich).

APC activity for the chromogenic substrates H-D-Val-Pro-Arg-p-nitroanilide (VPR) and H-D-Val-Leu-Arg-p-nitroanilide (VLR), each at 3.5 muM, was measured from progress curves of the release of p-nitroaniline at 405 nm. Values of kcat/KM for cleavage of the soluble fragment of PAR1 (10 muM), corresponding to the extracellular portion of the receptor (Figure 1D), were measured by a high-performance liquid chromatography assay using APC concentrations from 0.15 to 0.6 muM. All reactions were conducted in the presence of excess hirudin to eliminate possible cleavage by contaminating thrombin used to activate PC. Assays were performed under pseudo-first-order conditions with concentrations of PAR1 (10 muM) and VPR/VLR (3.5 muM) <KM Experimental conditions were as follows: 200 nM hirudin, 145 mM NaCl, 5 mM CaCl2, 0.1% polyethylene glycol 8000, 20 mM Tris, pH 7.5, at 37  C (PAR1) or 25  C (VPR and VLR). Measurements were performed in triplicate.

Activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) assays were used to determine the anticoagulant activities of the APC variants in plasma. Equal volumes (35 muL each) of normal plasma (King George Biomedical), STA-PTT A Reagent (Stago Diagnostica), and APC (10 nM) were preincubated at 37  C for 5 minutes, and clotting was initiated by adding 35 muL of 25 mM CaCl2. Clotting times were measured on a Stago Start coagulometer, and each measurement was performed in triplicate.

Inactivation of human FVa (Haematologic Technologies) by APC was monitored by following the loss of cofactor function in an assay that measures the residual activity of prothrombinase. Variable concentrations of APC (0.16-10 nM) were added to a mixture of FVa (1 nM) and phospholipids (50 muM) in a final volume of 10 muL, and the reaction was incubated for 7 minutes at 20  C. Each reaction sample was then mixed with 90 muL of a freshly prepared mixture composed of FXa (2 nM; Enzyme Research Laboratories), prothrombin (700 nM), and phospholipids (50 muM), followed by incubation for 3 minutes at 20  C. The activation of prothrombin was quenched by adding 190 nM of apixaban, prepared in 10 mM EDTA/tris-buffered solution. After a 15-fold dilution of the reaction samples, the formation of thrombin was quantified by following cleavage of the chromogenic substrate H-D-Phe-Pro-Arg-p-nitroanilide at 405 nm. Experimental conditions were 20 mM Tris, 145 mM NaCl, 5 mM CaCl2, 0.1% bovine serum albumin, pH 7.5, at 20  C. Each measurement was performed in triplicate.
RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

Among the 2 possible sites of cleavage at R41 and R46 in the extracellular domain of PAR1, thrombin cleaves only at R41 with a rate that is nearly diffusion-limited, and APC cleaves at both sites with very low catalytic efficiency. To better understand the molecular basis of this difference, several residues of APC were replaced with those of thrombin based on their specific interaction with PAR1. APCT99L carries the T99L replacement in the S2 site, which is expected to introduce a hydrophobic interaction with P40 of PAR1. APC37 replaces the entire 37-loop of APC with that of thrombin to remove potential steric clash with PAR1-R46 (Figure 1C). The hydrophobicity and architecture of the S2 site of APC were further optimized for PAR1 recognition with the combined replacement of the entire 60-loop and the T99L mutation in the APC60/T99L and APC37/60/T99L variants (Figure 1C). Notably, the T99L mutation was found to be necessary for expression when swapping the 60-loop. The specificity of wild-type (WT) APC for the soluble fragment of PAR1 corresponding to the extracellular portion of the receptor is very poor and ~500 000-fold lower than that of thrombin. Swapping the 37-loop produced a 3-fold increase in the value of kcat/KM, but introduction of the T99L mutation alone (APCT99L) or in combination with the 60-loop swap (APC60/T99L) produced increases of 10-fold and 40-fold, respectively (Table, Figure 2A). Addition of the 37-loop swap in the APC37/60/T99L mutant increased kcat/Km almost 80-fold (Table, Figure 2A).

Because thrombin only cleaves PAR1-R41, it is unclear how transferring structural elements of thrombin to APC may enhance specificity toward PAR1-R41 and compromise cleavage of PAR1-R46. To address this question, we tested the specificity of the mutants against a PAR1 peptide carrying the R41A mutation, PAR1R41A, which is cleavable only at PAR1-R46. Under conditions where cleavage of WT PAR1 by APC37, APC60/T99L, and APC37/60/T99L was completed, no significant cleavage of PAR1R41A was observed up to 72 hours (Figure 2B, C). In contrast, both APCWT and APCT99L cleaved PAR1R41A over this time frame. This suggests that the enhanced specificity toward PAR1 featured by the APC constructs, bearing the T99L mutation and swapping of the 37- and 60-loops with those of thrombin, comes from an increased preference for PAR1-R41 cleavage and compromised ability to cleave PAR1-R46. Swapping the S2 site of APC with that of thrombin in APC60/T99L and APC37/60/T99L compromises cleavage at PAR1-R46 and increases cleavage at PAR1-R41 up to 80-fold (Figure 2). Introducing the T99L mutation contributes to this effect, which is consistent with the contribution of residue 99 to the specificity of proteases involved in blood coagulation. Swapping the 37-loop of APC with that of thrombin in APC37 compromises cleavage of PAR1 at PAR1-R46 and slightly enhances cleavage at PAR1-R41 (Figure 2). The result is likely a consequence of removing the steric clash predicted to occur between R46 of PAR1 and K39 of APC (Figure 1A) and introduction of favorable contacts with the 37-loop of thrombin.

The specificity of trypsin-like proteases is influenced by the nature of the P2 residue at the site of cleavage. In the case of PAR1, this residue is Pro (P40) at the R41 site and Leu (L45) at the R46 site (Figure 1D). The Pro/Leu preference of the APC variants for the P2 position of substrate was further analyzed with the hydrolysis of the chromogenic substrates VPR and VLR (Table). APCWT cleaved VPR and VLR with similar kcat/KM values, but APCT99L and APC60/T99L showed nearly a 30-fold preference for VPR. Interestingly, APC37 was more effective than APCWT in cleaving PAR1 but 4-fold less active toward VPR or VLR, suggesting that the 37-loop of thrombin introduced into the APC scaffold assumes a conformation better suited for PAR1 recognition. Similar effects were observed with the APC37/60/T99L variant.

These mutations also compromise the ability of APC to inactivate FVa. The anticoagulant activity of APC in plasma was tested with the APTT assay, which measures the effectiveness of the clotting response. In agreement with previous reports, incubation of plasma with APCWT significantly prolonged the clotting time due to increased inactivation of FVa and FVIIIa (Figure 3A). Prolongation of the clotting time measured in the presence of APCT99L was slightly lower than APCWT, but that measured upon addition of APC37, APC60/T99L, and APC37/60/T99L was significantly compromised (Figure 3A). These findings confirm and expand on previous observations of compromised anticoagulant activity in APC variants carrying mutations in the 37- and 60-loops. The results of the APTT assay are also consistent with independent measurements of APC cleavage of FVa, where APC60/T99L was slightly less active than APCWT, while APC37 and APC37/60/T99L were significantly compromised (Figure 3B).

All PC mutants were activated by thrombin at comparable rates in the absence of thrombomodulin, while in the presence of cofactor, the 37- and 60-insertions significantly compromised the kcat/KM values (Supplementary Table). The results confirm the importance of these loops in promoting thrombomodulin binding reported previously.

We conclude that the increased hydrophilicity of the S2 site and unique residues of the 37-loop of APC are responsible for cleavage at PAR1-R46. Whether such APC mutants remain cytoprotective will await future cell-based and in vivo studies. We expect the cytoprotective signaling to depend on PAR1-R46 cleavage and that the mutants will lack cytoprotective properties. However, if the cytoprotective signaling is initiated irrespective of the PAR1 cleavage site and depends only on binding of the Gla domain to EPCR, then the mutants might display cytoprotective features.
