passages.text: Box C/D snoRNPs and MDT-15/MED15 regulate mitochondrial surveillance via fatty acid metabolism

Multicellular organisms constantly encounter biotic and abiotic stressors that threaten to disrupt their homeostasis. To counteract this, they have evolved a series of conserved defense networks which monitor organellar function and the accumulation of aberrant molecular signals. As mitochondrial dysfunction can lead to a variety of pathologies, including metabolic impairment, neurodegeneration, cardiovascular disease, cancer, and sensitivity to bacterial infections, understanding these mitochondrial surveillance pathways is crucial.

Previous research in our lab established that one such pathway, the Ethanol Stress and Response Element (ESRE), was activated by a broad range of stresses, including exposure to the Gram-negative, opportunistic human pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa. In this report we show that MDT-15 and its downstream effectors, fatty acid desaturases FAT-6 and FAT-7, were required for ESRE activation. Interestingly, supplementation with fatty acids downstream of FAT-6/FAT-7 activity, from C. elegans' PUFA pathway, rescued ESRE activation in their knockdowns. Additionally, disruption of mdt-15, or its downstream effector fat-6 by RNAi diminished worm survival during exposure to P. aeruginosa, indicating that these genes play a role in host defense. Notably, box C/D snoRNPs complex that we previously identified as an activator of ESRE, is required for upregulation of fatty acid metabolism under ESRE-activating conditions. Our results provide insight into a novel interplay between box C/D snoRNPs, lipids, and MDT-15/Mediator in the regulation of mitochondrial surveillance and innate immunity.
Introduction

Mitochondria have long been characterized as "the powerhouse of the cell". While this oversimplification has some truth, these organelles also play key roles in regulating a variety of important biochemical processes that determine cellular health, which, if compromised, can lead to metabolic and cardiovascular disease, neurodegeneration, cancer, and aging. To maintain mitochondrial homeostasis, multicellular organisms have developed surveillance mechanisms and pathways that monitor a wide variety of signals, including mitochondrial bioenergetics, proteostasis, and key metabolites for disruptions that may indicate imbalanced homeostasis. In response to these signals, the cell activates gene expression programs that are coordinated between mitochondria and the nucleus, which are intended to regain a more normal function.

The most studied of these pathways is the mitochondrial unfolded protein response (UPRmt). This pathway activates the transcription factor ATFS-1, which upregulates mitochondrial chaperone effectors in response to mitochondrial dysfunction. The PINK1/Parkin pathway is responsible for autophagic degradation of mitochondria and selective respiratory chain turnover, which can be active in basal or stressed conditions. Another mitochondrial surveillance system is the Mitogen-activated protein kinase cascade (MAPKmt), defined by DLK-1/SEK-3/PMK-3 signaling cascade, which responds to mitochondrial bioenergetic abnormalities and plays a vital role in lifespan. As reactive oxygen species (ROS) are a common byproduct of mitochondrial function and play an important role in aging, levels of mitochondrial ROS are monitored via the Ethanol and Stress Response Element (ESRE) surveillance pathway.

The role of mitochondria in innate immunity has also been established, specifically in the context of host-pathogen interactions. It has been shown that activation of UPRmt provides resistance to agar-based infections with Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a Gram-negative opportunistic human pathogen commonly associated with hospital-acquired infections. Our lab has also established the importance of the ESRE pathway in host defense against P. aeruginosa liquid-based pathogenesis or acute iron removal.

Recently, there has been an increased appreciation for the diverse role of lipid metabolism in other cellular processes besides structural integrity, storage, energy production, aging, and the regulation of proliferation. Previously, it was demonstrated that monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFAs) play a role in innate immune activation in Caenorhabditis elegans. Additionally, the role of mitochondria in linking energy metabolism and innate immune activation has been highlighted through lipids such as ceramides, which can provide protection from toxin- or pathogen-induced mitochondrial damage.

Another interesting component that has been linked to immunometabolism are small nucleolar ribonucleoproteins (snoRNPs). Small non-coding RNAs (snoRNAs) in complex with snoRNPs guide nucleotide modification of ribosomal RNAs (rRNAs) or small nuclear RNAs (snRNAs). SnoRNPs are divided into two groups: those associated with box C/D or box H/ACA RNAs, which modify rRNA by performing 2'-O-methylation or pseudouridylation, respectively. A non-canonical role for snoRNPs was previously shown, where in response to doxorubicin-induced oxidative stress, Rpl13a (box C/D family) snoRNPs accumulate in the cytoplasm. Additionally, Rpl13a snoRNPs have been shown to regulate the response to lipotoxic and oxidative stress. Box C/D and box H/ACA snoRNAs have also been linked to innate immune activation, specifically by activating the protein kinase response (PKR), which can respond to dsRNA and metabolic stress. Previous research in our lab also identified a role for box C/D snoRNPs in regulation of the ESRE mitochondrial surveillance pathway.

Kwon et al. previously demonstrated the presence of a conserved, 11-nucleotide DNA element (TCTGCGTCTCT) known as the ESRE motif in genes upregulated in response to ethanol-induced stress (Fig. 1A; note that all motifs shown in Fig. 1 were derived de novo from the gene lists in relevant publications using MEME). In 2017, Tjahjono and Kirienko identified the same ESRE motif in genes upregulated in response to liquid-based pathogenesis with P. aeruginosa (LK-Pa), or acute iron removal, indicating the importance of ESRE in host defense (Fig. 1B). Follow-up research by Tjahjono et al. linked the ESRE pathway to mitochondrial surveillance, specifically to sensing increased ROS from aberrations in the mitochondrial electron transport chain.

C. elegans is a widely used model nematode, with several attractive features for studying innate immunity or surveillance pathways. Because it has been used in many subdisciplines of biology, it is very well understood and has many favorable characteristics, including incredibly well-studied development, neurology, aging, and infectious diseases. It has some of the best genetic tools of any model organism. Its small size and short generation time facilitate high-throughput experiments and substantial automation, which provide robust data. Its innate immune system shows significant conservation with a broad variety of other metazoans, including mammals, resulting in general applicability of discoveries about host-pathogen interactions. Finally, C. elegans is naturally a bacterivore. In most cases, it can be infected by merely feeding it a pathogen of interest. Additionally, since ingestion and infection are natural processes, it has evolved robust self-defense pathways to limit bacterial infection.

In this study, we identify the role of fatty acids and box C/D snoRNPs in mitochondrial surveillance activation and host defense. The evolutionarily-conserved mediator subunit MDT-15/MED15, which is a major regulator of lipid metabolic processes, and its downstream effectors FAT-6 and FAT-7 were required for mitochondrial ESRE, UPRmt, and MAPKmt activation. Additionally, we demonstrated that fatty acids from C. elegans' polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA) synthesis pathway are indispensable specifically for ESRE but not for UPRmt or MAPKmt activation. Furthermore, we show that MDT-15 and FAT-6 are necessary for host defense against P. aeruginosa liquid-based pathogenesis, in a PMK-1-independent manner. Moreover, we reveal a non-canonical role for snoRNPs in the regulation of fatty acid metabolism through FAT-7. Finally, we demonstrate a regulation of MDT-15 by box C/D snoRNPs as well as regulation of box C/D snoRNPs by MDT-15.
RESULTS
The evolutionarily conserved mediator subunit MDT-15/MED15 is required for ESRE activation

While investigating the biology underlying the host response to P. aeruginosa in Liquid Killing, we previously carried out a high-throughput screen to identify small molecules that increase C. elegans survival. Five of the hits we identified showed signs of stimulating host innate immunity, with LK56 providing the most protection. Although transcriptional profiling was performed on LK56-treated worms, and the compound was shown to depend on MDT-15/MED15 for its activity, a clear mechanism of action was not identified.

To uncover the potential mechanism of LK56-mediated rescue, we analyzed upstream regulatory sequences from genes upregulated by LK56 using RSAT and MEME. Analyses revealed significant enrichment of the ESRE motif (30.7%) in their promoters (Fig. 1C). Similar sequence analyses of genes differentially regulated by LK34 and LK38 also showed enrichment for the ESRE motif, albeit at lower rates (22.6% and 19.8%, respectively, compared to ~8% of the genome as a whole) (Table S1 and S2). Gene ontology analysis of LK56-upregulated genes using WormCat found enrichment of genes involved in lipid metabolism, detoxification, and pathogen response (Fig. 1D). This was consistent with previous research in the Kirienko lab showing that LK56 provided increased resistance to Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Enterococcus faecalis, and Staphylococcus aureus. Since LK56-responsive genes exhibited enrichment for the ESRE motif, and LK56 activity depends on MDT-15, we hypothesized that activation of ESRE genes may similarly rely on MDT-15. To test this, RNAi was used to knock down mdt-15 in a C. elegans strain carrying a GFP reporter driven by three tandem repeats of the ESRE motif (3XESRE::GFP). This reporter strain was exposed to rotenone, which is known to activate ESRE. GFP expression was virtually abolished on mdt-15(RNAi), even in the presence of rotenone (Fig. 1E-F). These results indicate that the evolutionarily-conserved mediator subunit MDT-15 is required for ESRE activation in response to mitochondrial damage.
FAT6 and FAT-7 link ESRE activation to lipid metabolism

Amongst its many targets, MDT-15/MED15 has previously been shown to regulate the expression of the Delta9-fatty acid desaturases FAT-6 and FAT-7. These proteins convert the saturated stearic acid (SA) into monounsaturated oleic acid (OA) (Fig. 2A), with the latter being involved in innate immunity. Desaturation of SA is required for proper membrane function, and MUFAs play key roles in lipid distribution, fat storage, and signaling. For this reason, we tested the effect of RNAi targeting fat-6 and fat-7 on GFP expression in rotenone-treated 3XESRE::GFP worms (Fig. 2B-C). Similar to MDT-15, FAT-6 and FAT-7 were required for full activation of the ESRE reporter. This effect was also observed for the expression of native ESRE genes using qRT-PCR (Fig. 2D), confirming that MUFA production is necessary for activation of mitochondrial surveillance.

Multicellular organisms have numerous mitochondrial surveillance pathways, responding to a variety of stresses. We tested whether MDT-15, FAT-6, and FAT-7 also regulate the mitochondrial unfolded protein response (UPRmt) or the mitochondrial MAPK cascade (MAPKmt). RNAi was used to knock down mdt-15, fat-6, or fat-7 in reporter strains carrying Phsp-6::GFP (UPRmt) or Ptbb-6::GFP (MAPKmt) that were activated by spg-7(RNAi) (Fig. 3A-B). All three genes were required for activation of UPRmt, while only mdt-15 and fat-6 were required for MAPKmt activation (Fig. 3C-D). The decrease in reporter activation for either pathway after targeting fatty acid metabolism was significantly less than for ESRE activation (Fig. S1). Interestingly, activation of the MAPKmt pathway by mdt-15(RNAi), fat-6(RNAi), or fat-7(RNAi) under basal conditions was comparable to spg-7(RNAi) induction (Fig. 3E-F), indicating significant differences in the function of this pathway in mitochondrial surveillance programs.
Oleic acid plays a role in ESRE pathway activation

FAT-6 and FAT-7 are known to be involved in OA production and innate immune activation. To determine whether OA production is sufficient to rescue ESRE activation, RNAi was used to knock down mdt-15, fat-6, and fat-7 in the 3XESRE::GFP reporter reared on media containing 500 muM OA (Fig. 4A-C). Similar results were seen regardless of whether the non-ionic surfactant Tergitol (NP-40) was added to the medium (compare Fig. S2A-C and Fig. 4B-D). Supplementation of OA to the treatment enhanced rotenone-triggered ESRE activation when fat-6 or fat-7, but not mdt-15, were knocked down by RNAi (Fig. 4B-D). Interestingly, OA supplementation enhanced rotenone-triggered ESRE activation in worms reared on the empty RNAi vector, suggesting that OA limitation normally curtails ESRE mitochondrial surveillance even when lipid metabolism is not disrupted. However, in the absence of mitochondrial stress triggered by rotenone, OA was not sufficient to induce ESRE pathway activation (Fig. S3), indicating that OA augments activation under stress.
Fatty acids downstream of oleic acid are required for mitochondrial ESRE activation

The rescue of the reduction in rotenone-mediated GFP expression in fat-6(RNAi) and fat-7(RNAi) by OA indicated that it functions downstream of or in parallel to these genes. To examine the role of downstream fatty acids in the C. elegans PUFA pathway (Fig. 5A) in mitochondrial surveillance, the 3XESRE::GFP reporter strain was reared on media containing 500 muM linoleic acid (LA), 500 muM gamma-linolenic acid (GLA), or 500 muM arachidonic acid (ARA), and mdt-15, fat-6, or fat-7 were knocked down using RNAi. ESRE expression was then measured after rotenone induction at different time points (Fig. 5B-D, Fig. S4A-F). Supplementation with any of these fatty acids improved ESRE expression after rotenone exposure. For this reason, we also examined rotenone-mediated expression of native ESRE genes during ARA supplementation (Fig. 5E). Expression of these genes was upregulated, indicating the importance of fatty acids in ESRE effector gene activation.

As mdt-15 and fat-6 were involved in spg-7(RNAi)-mediated activation of UPRmt and MAPKmt, we tested whether supplementation with these fatty acids would rescue activation of these reporters after mdt-15, fat-6, or fat-7 were knocked down. In contrast to observations from the ESRE reporter, OA, LA, or ARA supplementation did not increase spg-7(RNAi)-mediated UPRmt reporter expression (Fig. S5-S7). In contrast, OA decreased UPRmt activation in fat-7(RNAi) and the empty vector (EV) control, LA decreased UPRmt in the EV control, and ARA supplementation decreased UPRmt in fat-6(RNAi). Supplementation with OA, LA, or ARA had no effect on basal UPRmt expression.

Supplementation of media with OA, LA, or ARA had no apparent effect on spg-7(RNAi)-mediated induction of the MAPKmt reporter (Fig S5-S7). In contrast, RNAi-mediated upregulation of the MAPKmt reporter under basal conditions was attenuated in fat-6 or fat-7 RNAis supplemented with OA and EV or mdt-15 RNAis supplemented with ARA. Supplementation with LA did not have overt effects on basal expression of the MAPKmt reporter. Finally, the expression of UPRmt and MAPKmt effector genes was examined in the presence of ARA under rotenone-induced mitochondrial stress (Fig. S8). ARA supplementation either decreased or did not affect UPRmt and MAPKmt effector gene expression, further supporting that fatty acid-mediated rescue is specific for the ESRE pathway.
MDT-15/MED15 and FAT-6 are required for host defense against Pseudomonas aeruginosa in liquid pathogenesis model

Mitochondrial ESRE surveillance is activated in response to liquid-based P. aeruginosa pathogenesis (LK-Pa). Since MDT-15, FAT-6, and FAT-7 play a role in mitochondrial ESRE activation, their effect on host defense was measured. glp-4(bn2) worms were reared on mdt-15(RNAi), fat-6(RNAi), or fat-7(RNAi) and then examined in LK-Pa. Worms reared on mdt-15(RNAi) and fat-6(RNAi) from the L1 (Fig. S9A) or the L3 stage both showed increased sensitivity to LK-Pa (Fig. 6A).

To rule out the possibility that this effect was non-specific, glp-4(bn2) worms reared on RNAi targeting mdt-15, fat-6, or fat-7 were tested for sensitivity to Liquid Killing conditions where E. coli was substituted for P. aeruginosa (LK-Ec). Worms reared on RNAi from the L3 stage and exposed to LK-Ec (Fig. 6B) were indistinguishable from wild-type worms, suggesting that the sensitivity was specific to LK-Pa. As RNAi of these genes causes developmental changes (i.e., RNAi-treated worms are smaller in length and width), future experiments using RNAi feeding were performed starting at the L3 stage to limit these effects.

Previously, Pukkila-Worley et al. demonstrated that mdt-15 is involved in the regulation of innate immune activation and detoxification stress response. Using RNAi and an irg-4::GFP transcriptional reporter, they screened for candidate genes involved in the regulation of PMK-1/p38-dependent gene expression. mdt-15 was a hit in this screen, and gene expression analyses showed that mdt-15(RNAi) reduced expression of several PMK-1/p38-dependent genes, including genes important for resistance to P. aeruginosa.

However, it is unlikely that MDT-15 is regulating innate immune responses with the same mechanisms in Liquid and Slow Killing assays; previous research indicated that innate immune responses defending the host against P. aeruginosa in these two assays don't generally overlap. For example, PMK-1/p38 MAPK is critical for resistance in Slow Killing assays but PMK-1 activity is detrimental in Liquid Killing. Similarly, box C/D snoRNP genes promoting C. elegans survival in Slow Killing reduce survival in liquid-based pathogenesis.

To address this, we tested the effect of RNAi targeting mdt-15, fat-6, or fat-7 with RNAi starting at L3 stage (Fig. 6C)) on host defense against agar-based P. aeruginosa (SK-Pa) pathogenesis. Only mdt-15(RNAi) increased susceptibility to killing by P. aeruginosa in the agar pathogenesis model. The fact that MDT-15 is required for survival in both LK-Pa and SK-Pa is likely due to its critical role as a regulator of multiple pathways, including ESRE and the PMK-1/p38 pathway, which are crucial for host defense in LK-Pa and SK-Pa, respectively.
Oleic acid promotes innate immune activation through induction of PMK-1/p38 pathway effectors

As ESRE activation was observed in fat-6 and fat-7 RNAis in the presence of exogenous OA, we hypothesized that this OA-mediated ESRE activation would increase the survival of mdt-15 or fat-6 RNAis in LK-Pa. To test this, worms were fed fat-6 or mdt-15 RNAis and reared on agar plates with or without 500 muM OA supplementation. At the young adult stage, worms were tested in LK-Pa assays and death was measured at different timepoints (Fig. 6D).

Unexpectedly, OA supplementation led to higher, rather than reduced, susceptibility to killing by LK-Pa in EV and mdt-15 RNAis. The likeliest explanation for this is that OA supplementation triggered activation of the PMK-1/p38 MAPK pathway, which is known to reduce survival in Liquid Killing. To test this, PMK-1-dependent gene expression was evaluated in mdt-15(RNAi) or EV control worms with or without OA in the LK-Pa assay (Fig. 6E). Consistent with results from Pukkila-Worley et al., RNAi targeting mdt-15 decreased expression of PMK-1/p38 effectors. However, OA supplementation rescued expression of these immune effectors, even in LK-Pa conditions, where this pathway is normally inactive.

Since OA supplementation increased killing in EV and mdt-15(RNAi) during LK-Pa due to increased PMK-1-dependent gene expression, we hypothesized that downstream fatty acids would elicit similar results. To test this, we reared L3-stage worms on mdt-15(RNAi) or fat-6(RNAi) supplemented with 500 muM LA, 500 muM GLA, or 500 muM ARA. At the young adult stage, worms were tested in LK-Pa and death was measured. Supplementation with these fatty acids increased death by LK-Pa in worms treated with the EV control (Fig. S9B). qRT-PCR was used to measure PMK-1/p38 targets in worms fed with EV under basal conditions after supplementation with ARA (Fig. 6F). Similarly to OA, supplementation with ARA upregulated basal expression of PMK-1-dependent genes. Interestingly, when fatty acids were supplemented to EV, mdt-15, and fat-6 RNAis and treated with LK-Ec, we saw an increase in mdt-15 survival (Fig. S9C). This can be explained by the fact that PMK-1/p38 activation is not detrimental in the LK-Ec model as there is no pathogenesis that places additional burden onto host metabolism.
Small nucleolar ribonucleoproteins play a role in innate immunity and mitochondrial surveillance through fatty acids

Previously, Tjahjono et al. described a non-canonical role for box C/D small nucleolar ribonucleoproteins (snoRNPs) in mitochondrial surveillance and innate immunity. Box C/D snoRNPs FIB-1, NOL-56, and NOL-58 act as a molecular switch that turns on mitochondrial surveillance (ESRE and UPRmt) whilst repressing the PMK-1/p38 innate immune pathway. Given that OA is required for ESRE activation and snoRNPs are involved in mitochondrial surveillance, including ESRE activation, we tested the effect of exogenous OA supplementation on snoRNP knockdowns. We supplemented fib-1, nol-56, and nol-58 RNAis with 500muM OA on agar as well as 300 muM OA in the liquid treatment and observed the impact on rotenone-induced ESRE activation. Our results indicate that OA partially rescues ESRE activation in all snoRNP knockdowns (Fig. 7A-C), similar to its effect on knockdowns of fat-6 and fat-7. This suggests that OA may function downstream or in parallel to snoRNPs pathway. Additionally, we supplemented linoleic acid (LA), gamma-linolenic acid (GLA), and arachidonic acid (ARA) as previously described to fib-1(RNAi) to evaluate their effect on ESRE activation. Our results show that these supplementations all rescued ESRE activation (Fig. 7D-F).

Tjahjono et al. had shown that box C/D snoRNPs are required for activation of mitochondrial surveillance. We decided to evaluate the effect of OA, LA, and ARA supplementation on UPRmt and MAPKmt activation in fib-1(RNAi) (Fig. S10A-B). Our results show that, in this background, supplementation of OA and LA decreased spg-7(RNAi)-induced UPRmt activation in the EV control while ARA did not elicit any effect (Fig. S10C). Additionally, supplementation of OA, LA, and ARA did not affect spg-7(RNAi)-induced MAPKmt activation (Fig. S10D) or basal expression of UPRmt nor MAPKmt (Fig. S10E-F). Altogether, these results strongly indicate a specific relationship between fatty acids, snoRNPs, and mitochondrial ESRE activation.
The stearoyl-coA desaturase FAT-7 is expressed in response to mitochondrial damage and P. aeruginosa infection

To assess whether fatty acid metabolism is affected under ESRE-inducing conditions, we used a worm strain (DMS303) carrying fat-7p::FAT-7::GFP multicopy array. We treated FAT-7::GFP worms with LK-Pa, SK-Pa, and their non-pathogenic counterparts, LK-Ec and SK-Ec, for 24 hours and then imaged after washing bacteria off. Our results show that FAT-7 is strongly upregulated in response to P. aeruginosa liquid-based pathogenesis, but not in response to agar-based pathogenesis (Fig. 8A-B). Additionally, we looked at the effect of mdt-15(RNAi) on FAT-7 activation in the LK-Pa assay and saw that knockdown of mdt-15 abolished FAT-7::GFP levels, consistent with the role of MDT-15 in the regulation of fatty acid metabolism (Fig. 8C-D).

To analyze the relationship between box C/D snoRNPs and fatty acid metabolism in ESRE regulation, we assessed FAT-7::GFP levels in RNAi knockdowns of fib-1, nol-56, and nol-58 in the LK-Pa assay. Interestingly, we saw that these RNAis led to significantly decreased FAT-7::GFP levels, revealing an unexpected connection between these pathways and indicating that snoRNPs function upstream of FAT-7 in ESRE regulation (Fig. 8E-F). Furthermore, treatment with mitochondrial stress inducer iron chelator 1,10-phenanthroline also resulted in high levels of FAT-7::GFP (Fig. 8G-H), strengthening the connection between mitochondrial surveillance and fatty acid metabolism.

To gain insight into the regulatory mechanism for FAT-7 by box C/D snoRNPs, we conducted qRT-PCR to look at fat-7 expression under fib-1(RNAi) in ESRE-activating conditions. In contrast with translational reporter results, fat-7 expression is upregulated upon fib-1(RNAi) (Fig. 8I). These results suggest that box C/D snoRNPs regulate FAT-7 on the translational level.

Since OA rescued ESRE activation in fat-7 and box C/D snoRNPs RNAis and it promoted PMK-1/p38 effector upregulation, we tested the effect of OA supplementation on FAT-7::GFP activation under fib-1, nol-56, and nol-58 knockdowns in the LK-Pa assay. Our results show that OA supplementation is not sufficient to rescue FAT-7::GFP activation in these knockdowns (Fig. S11).

Since our results showed that box C/D snoRNPs regulate ESRE pathway through FAT-7, we were interested in studying the relationship between lipid metabolism and box H/ACA snoRNPs. To test this, we assessed phenanthroline-induced FAT-7::GFP levels in RNAis targeting nola-3/Nop10, Y48A6B.3/Nhp2, K015.5/dyskerin or Y66H1A.4/Gar1. Our results indicate that Y48A6B.3/Nhp2 and nola-3/Nop10 knockdowns reduce FAT-7::GFP levels (Fig. 8J-K), albeit to a lesser extent than box C/D snoRNPs, suggesting that box H/ACA snoRNPs are less directly involved with the regulation of FAT-7.
Nuclear localization of FIB-1 is dependent on MDT-15

To uncover the connection between box C/D snoRNPs, FAT-7, and fatty acid metabolism, we used a worm strain (COP262) carrying fib-1p::FIB-1(genomic)::eGFP::fib-1 3' UTR single copy insertion. We reared FIB-1::GFP worms on EV, mdt-15, and fib-1 RNAis and examined their effect on basal FIB-1 expression. Our results indicate that mdt-15(RNAi) reduced the area of FIB-1 nuclei, uncovering an unanticipated regulatory mechanism of fatty acid metabolism for box C/D snoRNPs (Fig. 9A).

Since fatty acids downstream of FAT-6/FAT-7 were able to rescue ESRE activation in mdt-15, fat-6, and fib-1 knockdowns, we hypothesized that supplementation of the most downstream fatty acid could rescue FIB-1 expression in mdt-15(RNAi). To test this, we fed FIB-1::GFP worms EV or mdt-15 RNAis reared on either non-supplemented or 500 muM ARA-supplemented media. Non-supplemented worms were then treated with DMSO, and supplemented worms were treated with either DMSO or DMSO + 300 muM ARA. Our results show that fatty acid supplementation did not increase the level of nuclear FIB-1::GFP, suggesting that MDT-15 regulates it through a different mechanism. (Fig. 9B).
Discussion

In this study we found that MDT-15/MED15 and box C/D snoRNPs work together to modulate fatty acid metabolism and mitochondrial surveillance activation, likely via regulation of fatty acid metabolism. We also found that MDT-15 and downstream effectors are required for host defense against P. aeruginosa liquid-based pathogenesis. Using bioinformatics approaches (i.e. Wormcat, RSAT, and MEME SUITE) on immune-stimulating compound LK56, we found an enrichment of differentially upregulated lipid metabolism genes, which also contained the ESRE motif in their promoter sequences. Similar results were observed when we looked at differentially upregulated genes in response to P. aeruginosa liquid-based pathogenesis, indicating a strong connection between lipid metabolism and host defense. By using worm reporters, we demonstrate the involvement of MDT-15/MED15, FAT-6/SCD, and FAT-7/SCD in the regulation of mitochondrial ESRE, UPRmt, and MAPKmt pathways, strengthening the link between lipid metabolism in the regulation of mitochondrial surveillance. This was an interesting finding as the role of lipids, such as ceramide, in the regulation of mitophagy and activation of UPRmt during proteotoxic stress was established, but this area of regulation remained unknown in mitochondrial ESRE.

Using cell biology assays, we were able to determine that fatty acids from C. elegans' PUFA pathway play a vital role in mitochondrial ESRE activation, but not UPRmt or MAPKmt. Since MDT-15, FAT-6, and FAT-7 are required for UPRmt and/or MAPKmt, we hypothesized that exogenous supplementation of downstream fatty acids would be able to rescue activation under these RNAis as well. However, our results showed that supplementation failed to rescue UPRmt and MAPKmt activation, indicating this rescue is specific to ESRE. The most likely explanation for this is that ESRE exhibits a stronger sensitivity to ROS than UPRmt or MAPKmt. It has been shown that increased levels of long-chain fatty acids can affect mitochondrial redox activity and enhance the production of ROS at steady state respiration. This effect would be exacerbated during mitochondrial stress conditions, such as inhibition of Complex I by rotenone. With this in mind, supplementation of OA, LA, GLA, or ARA likely increases mitochondrial ROS production, which can induce ESRE activation even if there are low levels of MDT-15, FAT-6, and FAT-7. Additionally, when we supplemented these fatty acids, we saw earlier activation of 3XESRE::GFP by rotenone in our empty vector RNAi control, suggesting they could be inducing ROS, which in turn indirectly activates ESRE. Further experiments will need to be conducted to determine the exact mechanism by which these fatty acids rescue and promote early ESRE activation.

Given that various ESRE effectors are upregulated in response to P. aeruginosa liquid-based pathogenesis, we tested the effect of mdt-15, fat-6, and fat-7 RNAis on host defense in this context and observed their requirement for host survival. Additionally, we recapitulate published results by showing that mdt-15 is required for survival in P. aeruginosa agar-based pathogenesis. It is important to note that FAT-6 and FAT-7 have very similar roles in lipid metabolism, which often results in redundancy. In our case, fat-6 RNAi showed a stronger phenotype than fat-7 in the context of LK-Pa. Since our results showed rescue of ESRE activation by supplementation of OA, LA, GLA, and ARA, we hypothesized that this rescue in ESRE activation would be sufficient to promote host survival in LK-Pa. Our results showed the opposite effect, with higher death in supplemented worms, indicating our initial hypothesis was wrong. Published research has shown that stearidonic acid (SDA) and GLA are required for activation of PMK-1-dependent innate immune effectors. Similarly, we hypothesized that supplementation of OA, LA, GLA, and ARA could activate PMK-1-dependent innate immune effectors and lead to higher death in LK-Pa. Our results indicate that OA and the most downstream fatty acid, ARA, can induce PMK-1-dependent gene expression, providing an explanation for why supplemented worms died more than the non-supplemented cohort. Activation of PMK-1-dependent effectors leads to higher susceptibility to killing in LK-Pa likely because these demand important resources, such as chaperones, that would also be required for mitigating organellular damage elicited by pyoverdine.

In this study, we also explored the relationship between box C/D snoRNPs, mitochondrial surveillance, and lipid metabolism. Published research has demonstrated non-canonical roles for box C/D snoRNPs in the context of mitochondrial surveillance and innate immunity. Since fatty acids are vital for ESRE activation, as well as box C/D snoRNPs, we evaluated the effect of supplementation on RNAi of these components. Our results demonstrate that fatty acids can rescue ESRE activation in fib-1 RNAi, an important component of box C/D snoRNPs. Similarly to mdt-15, fat-6, and fat-7 RNAis, supplementation of these fats to fib-1 RNAi did not rescue activation of UPRmt nor MAPKmt pathways, indicating again this is specific for ESRE pathway. Our results provide a novel link between lipid metabolism and box C/D snoRNPs in the context of mitochondrial surveillance.

To explore this connection, we used worm reporters to conduct epistatic experiments for box C/D snoRNPs and lipid metabolism. Our results indicate that box C/D snoRNPs regulate expression of FAT-7 during P. aeruginosa liquid-based pathogenesis and mitochondrial damage. Furthermore, supplementation of exogenous OA does not rescue FAT-7 expression in mdt-15 nor fib-1 RNAi, indicating fatty acids are not a required component for proper fat-7 expression and/or translation. Previous studies have elucidated regulatory mechanisms for box C/D snoRNPs in the context of nucleolar localization. Our results indicate that basal FIB-1 expression is MDT-15-dependent, providing a novel regulatory mechanism for box C/D snoRNPs.

Investigation into the regulatory pathways involving box C/D snoRNPs may provide insight into the pathologies of various cancers that have been associated with misexpression of box C/D snoRNAs. Here, we focus on the regulation of lipid metabolism by box C/D snoRNPs, but snoRNPs are implicated in other pathways such as the PI3K/AKR/mTOR, MAPK, and p53-dependent apoptosis pathway, which if dysregulated, may result in apoptosis inhibition, increased proliferation, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT); factors that are associated with tumor development. Additionally, several box C/D snoRNAs have been identified to be diagnostic and prognostic markers of cancer progression and could serve as potential cancer treatment targets. Our research serves as a starting point for investigating the regulation of snoRNPs, potentially leading to therapies targeting tumor progression.
Materials and Methods
C. elegans Strains

All C. elegans strains were maintained on nematode growth medium (NGM) plates seeded with Escherichia coli strain OP50 as the food source and were maintained at 22 C, unless noted otherwise. C. elegans strains used in this study included N2 Bristol (wild-type) , SS104 (temperature-sensitive mutant that produces progeny at 15 C and is sterile at 25 C ) lglp-4(bn2)Il, WY703 lfdIs2 [3XESRE::GFP]; pFF4[rol-6(su1006)]l, SJ4100 lzcIs13 [Phsp-6::GFP]l, SLR115 ldvIs67 [Ptbb-6::GFP + Pmyo-3::dsRed]l, DMS303 lnIs590 [fat-7p::FAT-7::GFP + lin15(+)] Vl, and COP262 lknuSi221[fib-1p::FIB-1(genomic)::eGFP::fib-1 3' UTR + unc-119(+)]l.

Synchronized worms were prepared by hypochlorite isolation of eggs from gravid adults, followed by hatching of the eggs in pure S Basal. 6,000 synchronized L1 larvae were transferred onto 10 cm NGM plates seeded with OP50. After transfer, worms were grown at 22 C for 48 hours before experiments, or for three days for the next isolation of eggs. For synchronization of SS104 worms, 6,000 synchronized L1 larvae were transferred onto 10 cm NGM plates seeded with OP50 and grown at 15 C for five days for the next isolation of eggs. L4 hermaphrodite worms were used for all assays unless specified in the text.
Bacterial strains

RNAi experiments in this study were done using RNAi-competent E. coli (HT115-based) obtained from the Ahringer or Vidal RNAi libraries. All strains were sequenced prior to use. For experiments involving P. aeruginosa, the PA14 strain was used.
RNA interference protocol

RNAi-expressing E. coli were cultured and seeded onto NGM plates supplemented with 25 mug/mL carbenicillin and 1 mM IPTG. For RNAi experiments starting at L1, 1500 synchronized L1 larvae were transferred onto 6 cm RNAi plates and grown at 22 C for 48 hours prior to imaging, exposure to chemical treatment or pathogens. For double RNAi experiments, specifically pertaining to Phsp-6::GFP and Ptbb-6::GFP experiments, RNAi was mixed at a 3:1 ratio with spg-7(RNAi) or EV control respectively.

For RNAi experiments starting at L3, 6,000 synchronized L1 larvae were transferred onto 10 cm regular NGM plates seeded with OP50 and grown at 22 C for 22 hours until reaching the L3 stage. Worms were then washed off the plates, rinsed three times with S Basal, and transferred onto RNAi plates. These worms were then grown at 22 C for 24 hours on RNAi plates before use for experiments.
C. elegans chemical exposure assays

Synchronized L4-stage worms were washed from NGM plates seeded with E. coli OP50, HT115-based RNAi-expressing E. coli, or OP50-based RNAi-expressing E. coli into a 15 mL conical tube and rinsed three times. For experiments involving the use of 3XESRE::GFP strain, worms were sorted into a 96-well half-area plate (~100 worms/well), and the total volume per well, including treatment, was 100 muL. Treatment with rotenone (Sigma) was done at a final concentration of 25 muM per well. For liquid supplementation of fatty acids, a final concentration of 300 muM per well was used. For treatment with 1,10-Phenanthroline, a final concentration of 4 mM per well was used. DMSO was used as the solvent control for all of these treatments at a v/v ratio relative to the treatment.

For experiments involving the use of the FAT-7::GFP strain, worms were sorted into a 96-well full area plate (~150 worms/well) and a total volume per well of 160 muL including treatment. Worms were imaged with Cytation5 automated microscope every hour for eighteen hours at room temperature. At least three biological replicates were performed for each experiment.
C. elegans fatty acid supplementation assays

Fatty acids were obtained from Nu-Chek-Prep, Inc. and were prepared as previously described. Assays were performed by growing synchronized L1 worms on the indicated fatty acid or control media. Unless otherwise indicated, OA, LA, GLA, and ARA were used at a final concentration of 500 muM. Fatty acid supplementation assays recommend the addition of a surfactant, such as NP-40 (Tergitol), to the agar prior to autoclaving in order to increase the solubility of the fatty acid in the media. However, the fatty acid can also be delivered via DMSO as its vehicle. We got the same results on fatty acid supplementation experiments with the use of NP-40 and using DMSO as our vehicle for fatty acid supplementation (Fig. S2).
Quantitative reverse transcriptase PCR (qRT-PCR)

30,000 young adult worms were used for RNA extraction, and subsequent qRT-PCR was performed as previously described. Before RNA extraction, worms were reared on RNAi plates starting at the L1 stage, as previously described. For treatment with rotenone, L4-stage worms were washed off plates, rinsed three times, and were incubated for 8 hours in S Basal supplemented with 25 muM rotenone, 300uM fatty acid + 25uM rotenone, or a corresponding volume of DMSO control. For LK-Pa treatment, young adult worms were washed off plates, rinsed three times, and were sorted onto a 6 well plate (~10,000 worms/mL per well). Then, 2mL of LK medium mixed with P. aeruginosa PA14 were added to each well for a final volume of 3mLs and a final OD600 of 0.03. For each experiment, at least three biological replicates were performed.
C. elegans pathogenesis assays

P. aeruginosa liquid pathogenesis model (Liquid Killing or LK-Pa) was performed essentially as described. 25 synchronized young adult glp-4 mutants were sorted into each well of a 384-well plate. LK medium was mixed with P. aeruginosa PA14 (final OD600: 0.03) and then added into each well. Plates were incubated at 25  C. At different time points, plates were washed three times and worms were stained with SYTOX Orange nucleic acid stain (Invitrogen) for 12 hours to stain dead worms. Afterwards, plates were washed and then imaged using a Cytation5 automated microscope, and the fraction of dead worms was quantified autonomously with CellProfiler software. P. aeruginosa agar pathogenesis model (Slow Killing or SK-Pa) was performed as previously described. 50 young adult worms were transferred onto SK-Pa plates and incubated at 25  C. Worms were scored daily to obtain survival curves; dead worms were extracted from assay plates and worms that left the surface of the plate were censored from data analysis. P. aeruginosa liquid-based exposure to worms carrying fat-7p::FAT-7::GFP reporter (DMS303) was performed similarly to the LK-Pa assay. About 150 worms were sorted into each well of a 96-well full-area plate. Liquid Killing medium was mixed with P. aeruginosa PA14 (final OD600: 0.03) and then added into each well for a total volume of 160 uL. After 24 hours, bacteria were washed off the plates, and worms were imaged. Imaging and GFP quantification were performed with the Cytation5 automated microscope and Gen5 3.0 software.
Microscopy

For visualization of COP262 (FIB-1::GFP), worms were immobilized using 10mM levamisole and transferred onto a 3% noble agar slide. At least three biological replicates with 15 worms per replicate were imaged using a Zeiss ApoTome.2 Imager.M2, Carl Zeiss, Germany with 63x magnification. Hypodermic nuclei in the tail of each worm were imaged and quantified using the 10.2.0 version Imaris software.
Statistical Analyses

RStudio (version 4.3.0) was used to perform statistical analysis. One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed to calculate the significance of a treatment or a condition when there were more than three cohorts in the experimental setting. Statistically significant results as determined via ANOVA were then followed by Dunnett's test (R package DescTools, version 0.99.34) to calculate statistical significance or p values between each group compared to the control group. Dunnett's test was indicated in graphs as follows: no star = not significant, *p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, and *** p < 0.001.

passages.text: Calciphylaxis following liver transplantation in a patient with end-stage renal disease: A case report
BACKGROUND

Calciphylaxis, also called calcific uremic arteriolopathy, is characterized by microvascular calcification and occlusion, which is commonly seen in patients with end-stage renal disease (ESRD). Although several studies have demonstrated an association of calciphylaxis with ESRD, reports linking calciphylaxis to LT (LT) are scarce. This report presents a rare case of calciphylaxis in a patient who underwent LT, leading to microvascular occlusion and hyperbilirubinemia.
CASE SUMMARY

A 34-year-old man presented with a 7-day history of jaundice and severe bilateral leg pain. The patient had undergone LT and was put on hemodialysis for one year due to calcineurin inhibitor-induced ESRD. Physical examination revealed jaundice, leathery skin changes, severe muscle pain in both legs, and penile induration. Laboratory tests identified elevated bilirubin levels, gamma-glutamyltransferase, and alkaline phosphatase, while alanine aminotransferase and aspartate aminotransferase concentrations were within normal limits. Computed tomography (CT) revealed extensive calcifications in the subcutaneous tissue. Three-dimensional CT reconstruction indicated significantly reduced blood flow in the hepatic artery, primarily in the small to medium-sized branches. Contrast-enhanced ultrasonography confirmed hepatic ischemia, with no enhancement seen in hepatic artery branches. Liver biopsy specimen revealed no signs of rejection. The patient decided to receive conservative treatment and succumbed to the illness after six months.
CONCLUSION
This case indicates that calciphylaxis should be suspected in patients who have undergone LT with ESRD presenting with hyperbilirubinemia and skin lesions.

Core Tip: Calciphylaxis, a rare and life-threatening syndrome characterized by vascular calcification and tissue necrosis, predominantly affects end-stage renal disease patients. This case demonstrates the occurrence of calciphylaxis in a liver transplant recipient, presenting with multi-organ calcifications and hyperbilirubinemia caused by hepatic artery calcification. Early recognition of cutaneous and systemic calcification, combined with the management of metabolic dysregulation, is critical. This report indicates that calciphylaxis may be an unneglectable differential diagnosis for hyperbilirubinemia in transplant recipients and advocates for the development of preventive strategies in high-risk populations.
INTRODUCTION

Calciphylaxis is a rare and life-threatening syndrome which is common among patients with end-stage renal disease (ESRD), with few cases detected in individuals without renal failure. The disease is characterized by calcification and occlusion of small to medium-sized blood vessels, which causes ischemia and necrosis of the surrounding tissues. It is estimated that the incidence of calciphylaxis varies across populations, ranging from 1 to 35 cases per 10000 patients. Moreover, the overall prognosis is poor, with an average survival of approximately one year and an annual mortality rate exceeding 50%, most commonly induced by sepsis. Clinically, calciphylaxis presents as chronic, painful, and non-healing ulcerative skin lesions, that is commonly accompanied by leathery skin changes in the abdomen, axilla, and lower limbs regions. The key laboratory test findings include hyperparathyroidism, hypercalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, increased accumulation of calcium-phosphorous products, increased alkaline phosphatase levels, and elevated concentration of creatinine. Although skin biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosis, its diagnostic rate is reported to be 18%. In some cases, calcific deposits are detected in various organs, including the heart and eyes. However, reports linking calciphylaxis to liver transplantation (LT) are rare in clinical practice. Here, we present a case of hyperbilirubinemia secondary to calciphylaxis in a patient who underwent LT.
CASE PRESENTATION
Chief complaints
A 34-year-old man presented to our clinic with a 10-day history of jaundice and intermittent abdominal pain.
History of present illness

The patient received LT in 2018 to treat hepatocellular carcinoma. He had been undergoing hemodialysis for one year, attributing his ESRD to calcineurin inhibitor toxicity. The patient reported a 10 kg unintentional weight loss over the preceding three months. Ten days before presentation, he developed intermittent abdominal pain accompanied by severe bilateral leg pain. He was subsequently admitted to undergo further evaluation and management.

passages.text: History of past illness
On admission, the patient was receiving hemodialysis twice-weekly and had a history of hypertension for one year.
Personal and family history
The patient's personal and family history was negative.
Physical examination

On examination, jaundice accompanied with icteric sclera, severe muscle pain in both legs, and intermittent abdominal pain were observed. In addition, firm, tender subcutaneous nodules were detected in the abdominal region on palpation. Tactile pain and dusky skin discoloration were noted in the hip region. Additionally, penile induration and leathery skin changes in the axillary and hip areas were observed (Figure 1).
Leathery skin changes. A and B: Leathery skin changes in the axilla; C: Leathery skin changes in the hip area.
Laboratory examinations

Laboratory tests revealed significantly elevated serum bilirubin levels, as well as total bilirubin (423 mumol/L) and direct bilirubin (303 mumol/L). The concentrations of gamma-glutamyltransferase and alkaline phosphatase were elevated to 226 U/L and 261 U/L, while alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) were within normal limits. Creatinine levels were markedly elevated to 1047 mumol/L, and the parathyroid hormone level increased to 233 pg/mL. Serum calcium and phosphorous levels were 2.4 mmol/L and 2.7 mmol/L, respectively. Liver biopsy revealed decreased arteriole and severe cholestasis (Figure 2). The Banff rejection active index was 2/9 (portal inflammation: 1 point; endophlebitis: 0 points; cholangitis: 1 point), confirming the absence of allograft rejection.
Histological examination of liver biopsy specimen. A and B: Representative H&E staining of liver biopsy specimen. Scale bar = 20 mum (A), 50 mum (B).
Imaging examinations

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) revealed extensive calcifications in the subcutaneous tissues, bladder, penis, and bicuspid valve. Analysis of the three-dimensional CT reconstruction images demonstrated reduced blood flow in the hepatic artery, primarily in the small to medium-sized branches (Figure 3). Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography did not find evidence of obstruction in the common bile duct or hepatic ducts. Additionally, contrast-enhanced ultrasonography confirmed hepatic ischemia, with no enhancement in hepatic artery branches.

Computed tomography images. A: Calcification of the bicuspid valve; B: Calcium deposit in the liver; C: Calcification of the splenic artery; D: Calcification in the penis; E: Calcium deposition in the subcutaneous tissue of hip area; F: 3D reconstruction of computed tomography showing occlusion of branches of hepatic arteries.

passages.text: FINAL DIAGNOSIS

Considering the patient's history of ESRD, hemodialysis dependence, and extensive calcification, a diagnosis of calciphylaxis was made, together with application of the diagnostic criteria for calciphylaxis established by the Mayo Clinic.
TREATMENT

Sodium thiosulfate is the first-line treatment for calciphylaxis. Thus, the patient was scheduled to receive sodium thiosulfate at a dose of 25 g three times per week, combined with cinacalcet (30 mg daily) to manage hyperparathyroidism. His hemodialysis regimen was also adjusted, with both frequency and duration increased.
OUTCOME AND FOLLOW-UP
For personal reasons, the patient opted for conservative management at a local medical center. At the six-month follow-up, the patient succumbed to his illness.
DISCUSSION

In this paper, we report a patient with calciphylaxis following LT and ESRD, which caused hyperbilirubinemia post-transplant. The patient presented with severe leg pain, penile induration, and leathery skin changes. CT imaging revealed extensive calcification in the subcutaneous tissues, bladder, penis, and bicuspid valve. Moreover, there was a significant reduction in blood flow in the small to medium-sized hepatic artery branches. Further examination of liver biopsy found no evidence of allograft rejection. The patient opted to undergo conservative treatment and succumbed to the disease at the six-month follow-up.

Calciphylaxis, or calcific uremic arteriolopathy, is a severe condition that predominantly affects patients with ESRD, characterized by progressive vascular calcification and occlusion in small to medium-sized vessels. However, emerging evidence indicates that non-uremic calciphylaxis can occur in patients with preserved renal function. In the present case, we identified an unusual presentation of calciphylaxis in a liver transplant recipient, which indicated a complex interplay between hepatic dysfunction, dysregulated calcium-phosphorus metabolism, and endothelial injury. Currently, there is no internationally recognized standard diagnostic criteria for calciphylaxis. According to the guidelines by the Mayo clinic, skin biopsy and clinical criteria should be included in the diagnosis. In this case, the patient was receiving calcineurin inhibitors and other immunosuppressive agents. However, the ALT and AST were within normal limits, and histopathological examination showed no evidence of hepatocyte injury, thereby excluding drug-induced liver injury. Furthermore, serological tests for hepatitis B and C viruses were negative, and there was no histological evidence of viral hepatitis on biopsy. After exclusion of other causes, a diagnosis of calciphylaxis was made following the Mayo diagnostic criteria. The risk factors for calciphylaxis include ESRD, diabetes mellitus, hypercalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, hyperparathyroidism, elevated alkaline phosphatase, hepatobiliary disease, hypoalbuminemia, recurrent hypotension, and rapid weight loss, with ESRD being the most significant factor. Factors associated with LT, including immunosuppressive therapy, metabolic derangements, and systemic inflammation, have been reported to increase the risk of vascular calcification and endothelial dysfunction. Furthermore, studies have implicated hypoalbuminemia in the pathogenesis of calciphylaxis by altering calcium-phosphate homeostasis and increasing vascular mineral deposition. Deficiency of vitamin K-dependent matrix Gla protein, a key inhibitor of vascular calcification, can also promote vascular mineral deposition. Although direct evidence supporting the calciphylaxis-induced bile duct damage is lacking, further investigations into the hepatic manifestations of calciphylaxis in transplant recipients are advocated. Calcific deposits may occur in various organs, including the heart and eyes, leading to myocardial ischemia or visual impairment. However, reports of calciphylaxis occurring in the liver are few. Raza et al described a case of dystrophic calcification in a patient who underwent LT, inducing diffuse hepatic calcification, which was recognized as a differential diagnosis of calciphylaxis. In the present case, diffuse hepatic calcification was observed, accompanied with significant calcification in the cardiac valves, vessels, and penis. Dystrophic calcification is defined as a localized response to liver tissue damage, while calciphylaxis is a systemic vascular disorder driven by metabolic disturbances. The latter is severe, which can lead to high mortality. This case suggested that systemic vascular calcification may extend to hepatic arteries or the portal venous system, potentially impairing bile duct perfusion and contributing to biliary injury or cholestasis. However, the underlying mechanism of calciphylaxis are not clearly understood. The imbalance between calcification promoters and inhibitors, and vicious cycles of endothelial injury and microthrombosis may contribute to the pathogenesis of calciphylaxis.

passages.text: The prognosis of calciphylaxis is poor, underscoring the importance of preventive measures. Currently, no specific biomarker could be used for early detection, but monitoring serum levels of calcium, phosphate, and parathyroid hormone (PTH) could be helpful for identifying metabolic imbalances that predispose to calciphylaxis. Additionally, regular imaging every 6-12 months in high-risk patients could detect early vascular calcifications. Eliminating risk factors could prevent or slow the development of calciphylaxis, reduce the length and frequency of the hemodialysis for ESRD patients, correct hypercalcemia and hyperphosphatemia, lower PTH level, and avoid subcutaneous injection. Clinical studies have shown that supplementation of vitamin K (500 mug per day) slows the calcification by 6% at 3-year follow-up and help correct the disturbance of coagulation. Furthermore, the patient was treated with intravenous sodium thiosulfate at a dosage of 25 g three times a week after dialysis sessions, which is considered the first-line treatment for calciphylaxis. To achieve optimal clearance of uremic toxins and maintain electrolyte balance, the dialysis protocol was optimized to include extended sessions of 5 hours each, three times a week. But calciphylaxis completely resolved in only 26%-52% patients receiving sodium thiosulfate.
CONCLUSION

In this case report, we discuss the occurrence of calciphylaxis leading to hyperbilirubinemia in a patient who underwent LT and ESRD. The patient presented with characteristic skin lesions and widespread calcium deposits, suggesting that the presence of these symptoms should raise suspicion of calciphylaxis, and skin biopsy should be conducted as the golden standard. Considering the poor prognosis and unsatisfactory therapeutic effects, strategies for eliminating risk factors and preventing its occurrence need to be developed.

passages.text: The epigenetic potential of vitamin K2 in brain health
ABSTRACT

Vitamin K2 refers to a subfamily of vitamin K isoforms known as Menaquinones and, therefore, indicated as MK-n, the "n" indicating the number of isoprene units present in the side chain. Like the other members of the Vitamin K family, K2 is an enzymatic cofactor for the gamma-glutamyl carboxylase (GGCX). This enzyme's substrates, which carboxylate glutamic acid residues, are known as Vitamin K-dependent proteins (VKDPs). Besides being involved in bone homeostasis, vitamin K exerts its primary function in the coagulation process. More recently, a function of Vitamin K also in brain homeostasis has been claimed. In addition to these so-called "canonical" effects, recent research highlights the possibility that Vitamin K, particularly Vitamin K2 May 2001have or induce epigenetic effects through the modulation of DNA methylation, histone modifications, and microRNAs expression. This evidence seems particularly relevant in brain diseases, where epigenetics is gaining a central role as a modulator of multiple diseases-associated molecular metabolisms. The present review examines the recent literature (PubMed) to collect evidence for the role of Vitamin K2 in neurodegenerative diseases with the goal of fostering interest in its epigenetic potential.
Plain Language Summary

The term Vitamin K includes a family of molecules, with partially conserved structure, known to exert their primary function in the coagulation process (contributing to the activation of the coagulation factors) and to maintain the bone structure. It was recently suggested that Vitamin K could also exert other roles, mainly in contributing to brain health and to prevention of neurodegenerative diseases. Exploring this possibility, some research work suggests the possibility that this neuroprotective effect is mediated by epigenetic mechanisms. Epigenetics describes how modification of the DNA, not involving a change in the sequence (i.e. not causing DNA mutations) can modulate the expression of the genes, therefore modulating the production of the coded proteins and the cellular phenotype. These modifications include DNA methylation (the presence of a methyl-group, -CH3, in the cytosine residues of the DNA), histone modifications (i.e. the presence of methyl-, acethyl-, and other chemical residues in the histone proteins that bind DNA), and the expression of non-coding RNAs (mainly microRNAs, which reduce the translation of the messenger RNAs). The present review is based on the new evidence describing how Vitamin K effects, and specifically the K2 isoform, may be mediated by these epigenetic modifications in neurodegenerative disease, opening a new field of research.
Introduction

Vitamin K was first identified nearly a century ago, along with its critical role in coagulation. Since then, there has been a growing body of evidence supporting the role of vitamin K as a protective nutrient in aging and neurodegenerative diseases.
Nutritional sources of Vitamin K.

There are different isoforms of vitamin K, including phylloquinone, commonly known as vitamin K1, and menaquinones, collectively referred to as vitamin K2. Vitamin K2 represents a group of menaquinones (MK-n), differentiated by a common naphthoquinone ring structure and side chains of varying lengths made up of unsaturated isoprenoid units. The letter "n" indicates the number of isoprene units in the side chain. Phylloquinone is found in green leafy vegetables, such as spinach, and in some plant oils. The short-chain menaquinone MK-4 is present in animal-origin foods like eggs and chicken meat, while long-chain menaquinones, such as MK-7, MK-8, and MK-9, are predominantly found in fermented foods, notably cheese and natto (Figure 1).

Vitamin K serves as an essential cofactor for the enzyme gamma-glutamyl carboxylase (GGCX), which facilitates the post-translational gamma-carboxylation of specific glutamic acid residues in various vitamin K-dependent proteins (VKDPs). Beyond the well-known VKDPs involved in coagulation, key extrahepatic VKDPs include osteocalcin (OCN), which plays a critical role in bone mineralization, and matrix Gla-protein (MGP), a powerful inhibitor of vascular calcification. Recently, osteocalcin and other extrahepatic VKDPs have also been implicated in brain function, highlighting their broader biological importance.

Structural differences affect vitamin K bioavailability and activity. While both K1 and MK-7 are well absorbed, MK-7 has a significantly longer half-life, accumulating 7- to 8-fold with extended use. MK-7 is also more bioactive than K1 in fully carboxylated osteocalcin.
Canonical and non-canonical functions of vitamin K.

Beyond being a cofactor for GGCX, vitamin K2 also exerts non-canonical (GGCX-independent) functions, such as reduction of oxidative stress and inflammation, regulation of sphingolipid synthesis and mitochondrial function. Recently, a novel aspect of vitamin K2 has gained attention: its potential impact on epigenetic regulation (Figure 2).
The role of vitamin K2 in brain health

Vitamin K2 is broadly distributed throughout human tissues, including the central nervous system (CNS). Recent research has linked low vitamin K intake and poor extrahepatic vitamin K status not only to an increased risk of cardiovascular diseases but also to neurodegeneration.

Vitamin K is primarily present in the brain as MK-4 and dietary intake of any form, whether K1 or K2, can effectively increase the concentration of this isoform. Additionally, several extrahepatic VKDPs play critical roles in the central nervous system. For example, growth arrest-specific protein 6 (Gas6) promotes cell survival and myelination, protein S supports blood-brain barrier integrity, and MGP, an inhibitor of vascular calcification, is linked to vascular elasticity and cognitive performance.
Recent evidence highlights vitamin K2's key role in brain health and neurodegeneration, through both GGCX-dependent and independent mechanisms.

Apart canonical actions, based on the GGCX of VKDPs, vitamin K exerts also non-canonical functions GGCX independent (Figure 2). It is now well established the role of Vitamin K in biosynthesis of sphingolipids, widely present in brain cell membranes and key factors in maintaining the neuro-physiological functions. Moreover, increasing evidence underline both anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties of Vitamin K2, together with the ability to counteract the mitochondrial dysfunction. In addition, recent findings showed that vitamin K2 (mainly MK-4) after the reduction to hydroquinone by Ferroptosis suppressor protein 1 (FSP1), has a potent anti-ferroptotic effect, by trapping free radicals so reducing lipid peroxidation.

Recently, the epigenetic effect of vitamin K has been suggested as a new non-canonical function, even if in depth studies on the mechanisms and vitamin-mediated epigenetic alterations are still to be investigated.
Vitamin K2 and neurodegenerative disease.

The neuroprotective properties of vitamin K2 have recently been confirmed through both in vitro and in vivo research. Specifically, a very recent study provides compelling evidence that long-term low vitamin K (LVK) intake adversely affects hippocampal-dependent cognitive functions in C57BL/6 mice. These findings suggest that LVK impairs neurogenesis and promotes neuroinflammation. Additionally, the observed sex differences - with male mice showing lower survival rates, reduced body weight gain, and lower MK-4 concentrations - indicate that males may be more vulnerable to Vitamin K deficiency. Overall, these results not only align with previous human observational data but also highlight the need for more research into the biological mechanisms by which vitamin K supports brain health. Its potential role in the pathophysiology of neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and multiple sclerosis (Figure 3), is explored further below.
Vitamin K2 in multiple sclerosis

Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic demyelinating disorder affecting individuals aged 20-40 years, with higher prevalence in women. MS is considered an autoimmune disease and is characterized by demyelination, inflammation, and neuroaxonal damage, driven by inflammatory cytokines and reactive oxygen species. Emerging evidence highlights a potential role of vitamin K2 in MS.

The epidemiological data showed that serum vitamin K2 levels were more than three times higher in healthy controls compared to MS patients. Recent research has also identified a link between MS progression and reduced microbial production of vitamin K2. The role of vitamin K2 in MS development and progress deserves further research.
Limitations and future directions

Currently, the data regarding the implications of vitamin K2 in MS are extremely limited and obtained by observational and/or experimental studies. Large prospective epidemiological studies and RCTs are warranted to fully elucidate the exact role of vitamin K2 in MS.
Vitamin K2 in Parkinson's disease

Parkinson's disease (PD) is one of the most prevalent neurodegenerative disorders, yet its pathogenesis remains poorly understood. PD pathogenesis is primarily associated with oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and inflammation. Among these factors, neuroinflammation plays a particularly critical role in PD progression as evidenced by studies showing a lower incidence of PD in long-term non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug users.
Vitamins are well known for their anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties and have been suggested as a potential neuroprotective therapeutic approach, including PD.

Observational studies revealed that vitamin K levels in human plasma were inversely associated with various biomarkers of inflammatory factors. Additionally, unpublished research suggests that vitamin K2 significantly improves behavioral disorders in a rotenone-induced rat model of PD.

Epidemiological research on vitamin K2 in PD is limited. A case-control study revealed an association between vitamin K2 deficiency and PD progression, suggesting its potential as a diagnostic biomarker. Serum vitamin K2 levels were significantly lower in PD patients than in healthy controls and declined further with disease severity.

Mitochondrial dysfunction, linked to PD for nearly 40 years, is supported by the growing evidence. Genetic defects like PINK1 and Parkin mutations further impair mitochondrial function in PD patients. Vitamin K2 has shown the ability to restore mitochondrial function in PINK1 mutant models. It improved electron transport and increased ATP production. Consequently, vitamin K2 improved locomotor function in adult PINK1 and parkin mutant flies and has been suggested as a potential therapeutic option for PD patients with PINK1 or parkin deficiencies. Currently, recruitment is planned for the clinical study (DRKS00019932), to investigate the effects of vitamin K2 in genetically determined PD associated with mitochondrial dysfunction.
Emerging research also highlights the role of VKD protein OCN as a promising neuroprotective factor in PD. OCN administration improved motor function and reduced neuronal loss in PD rat model.
These findings collectively highlight the promising role of vitamin K2 in developing novel therapeutic strategies for PD.
Limitations and future directions

The data regarding vitamin K2 in PD are derived by experimental studies and/or observational studies and therefore preclude any causality. Moreover, the associations examined are mainly with surrogate endpoints and not clinically hard endpoints. Since vitamin K2 is a safe supplement, future, large RCTs examining the possible beneficial role of vitamin K2 in cognitive function, quality of life and longevity in PD patients might shed some light in this area.
Vitamin K2 in Alzheimer's disease

Accumulating evidence suggests that vitamin K has a protective effect against the progression of Alzheimer's disease (AD) by modulating several cellular mechanisms, including neuroinflammation, sphingolipid metabolism, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial dysfunction.

Dietary intake of vitamin K1 (assessed by food questionnaires or measuring circulating phylloquinone levels) has been directly correlated with memory function, suggesting a causal relationship between vitamin K and cognitive function. Since the main dietary source of vitamin K1 is green leafy vegetables, this correlation might also be an epiphenomenon reflecting healthy lifestyle and these studies did not assess the forms and levels of vitamin K in the brain. To address these issues, the Rush Memory and Aging Project showed that increased brain MK-4 concentrations were associated with a 17%-20% reduction in the likelihood of dementia or mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and lower AD global pathology scores.

One of the most prominent pathophysiologic pathways underlying the onset and progression of AD is arterial stiffness. The ARIC (Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities - Neurocognitive Study) study showed that among subjects >67 years old, those in the highest quartile of carotid-femoral pulse wave velocity (cfPWV) experienced a higher rate of white matter hyperintensities, decreased total brain volumes, and poorer performance scores in executive function, processing speed, and global cognition, which were independent of age, sex, hypertension, and blood pressure. In agreement with these results, a meta-analysis of 38 studies and 43,115 patients showed that PWV was negatively associated with general cognition, executive function, and memory status, and it has been calculated that each 1 m/s increase in PWV increased the risk of cognitive impairment by 3.9.

Vitamin K antagonists (VKAs), an "old-fashioned" class of anticoagulant drugs, which reduce blood clotting by antagonizing vitamin K recycling and metabolism, might increase the risk of cognitive impairment up to 15%. Long-term use of these agents in patients with normal cognitive function at baseline is associated with worsening of visual memory and verbal fluency. The deleterious effects of VKAs on the duration of focal cerebral atrophy are dose- and time dependent. Based on these data, several studies have highlighted the beneficial role of vitamin K2 supplementation in vascular health and arterial stiffness prevention, mainly via downregulation of circulating dephosphorylated, uncarboxylated Matrix Gla protein (dp-ucMGP). Given that stiffening of cerebral arteries is strongly associated with the progression of cognitive decline, vitamin K2 presents a promising, safe, and well-tolerated treatment option for AD prevention.
Limitations and future directions

There are various limitations regarding the data on the association of vitamin K2 and AD that should be acknowledged. These data are derived from observational studies, which preclude any causality; moreover, as has been mentioned before, the association between dietary intake of vitamin K1 and cognitive function might be an epiphenomenon of a healthy, plant-based diet. Finally, the data are mainly preclinical and human data are sparse and indirect. Future, large randomized controlled trials examining the potential effect of vitamin K2 supplementation on cognitive function in AD patients are needed in order to draw definite conclusions.
Vitamin K2 in cardiovascular diseases

It is now largely recognized that maintaining cardiovascular health may be beneficial in mitigating the progression of neurodegenerative diseases, since these pathologies share many common risk factors. The first epidemiologic study to indicate the pivotal role of vitamin K consumption in cardiovascular prevention was the Rotterdam study, showing that among 4807 subjects with no preexisting CVD, only vitamin K2 intake was significantly and inversely associated with all-cause mortality and severe aortic calcification. In a randomized control trial (RCT) Knapen et al. showed that among postmenopausal women, 3-year supplementation with 180 mug/day of MK-7 significantly improved arterial stiffness, which was even more pronounced in those who had higher baseline arterial stiffness.

Data from the Danish Diet, Cancer, and Health Study in 53,372 participants free of CVD, which were followed up for two decades, showed that high daily vitamins K1 and K2 were associated with a 21% and 14% lower risk of hospitalization due to atherosclerotic CVD, respectively. Similarly, supplementation with vitamin K2 (720 mug daily) and vitamin D (25 mug daily) versus placebo for 2 years patients with established coronary artery calcification (CAC), significantly delayed the valve calcification process.

CKD patients carry a heavy CV burden which is partially attributed to the accelerated vascular calcification, which occurs even at early stages. The KING trial (Vitamin K2 in Renal Graft) showed that 8-week daily MK-7 supplementation (360 mug/day) in 60 kidney transplant recipients reduced cfPWV by 14.2%, through a 40% improvement in subclinical vitamin K deficiency. Another RCT involving 40 kidney transplant recipients found that a 12-week MK-7 supplementation significantly decreased dp-ucMGP levels and arterial stiffness. Similarly, a study by Naiyarakseree et al. evaluated MK-7's effects in 96 hemodialysis patients with established arterial stiffness at baseline and found that 24 weeks of MK-7 supplementation (375 mug/day) reduced cfPWV in participants with diabetes mellitus by 10.0%. It has been calculated by meta-analyses that vitamin K supplementation reduces vascular calcification by 9.1% through a 44.7% reduction of dp-ucMGP levels, which still is modest. In addition, VKDPs were associated with a 0.45-fold lower risk of cardiovascular disease and mortality.

passages.text: Limitations and future directions

Although these results seem promising, these RCTs presented drawbacks and limitations, including the small sample size, the short follow-up period, the large heterogeneity of design, and the lack of clinical hard endpoints. Currently, well-designed trials in various populations, including CKD, are conducted. The results of these trials are expected to improve our understanding of the area of vitamin K2 in CVD.
